By 1918, the use of new weapons in new ways, and the 
novel and more sustainable operational approach the 
Allies pursued, were important factors in breaking the 
trench stalemate and restoring mobility to the battlefield. 
We must not get carried away by this. This was no 
Blitzkrieg. Neither the German offensives of spring 1918 
nor the Allied one of the Hundred Days were as fluid as 
the campaigns of 1939-41, nor even those of the early 
months of the fighting in 1914. A much better analogy 
would be the grinding, rolling attrition of June to mid-
August 1944 in Normandy. Nonetheless, in the course of 
three months in the late summer and autumn of 1918, the 
allies advanced up to eighty miles and broke the back of 
the German army, capturing 385,000 German prisoners, 
almost as many men as the German army’s total 
casualties at Stalingrad. Learning had made a direct and 
observable contribution to improved force employment 
and victory. Learning was a whole new fighting front of 
the First World War, one where the scientists and military 
intellectuals of both sides competed with all the effort 
and determination displayed in later famous measure/
counter-measure races such as the Battle of the Atlantic. 
The simple fact of the matter is that the Germans lost.
Why was this? Some of it comes down to things the Allies 
were doing right, of course, but some of it also down to 
things the Germans were doing wrong. There were three of 
these: 1) centralised control 2) poor information flow and 
so bad decisions 3) a fundamental misconception running 
through the German army. Let’s take these in turn.
The German army of the two world wars has a reputation 
for flexibility based in a system of decentralised command, 
known as Auftragstaktik or, in modern jargon, ‘mission 
command’. This is unmerited. In fact, a very high degree 
of central control was a feature of German command 
throughout almost all the First World War. Only during the 
war’s first weeks, when Moltke the Younger was so far out 
of his depth that he exercised no grip at all, and for a few 
months’ honeymoon period in the second half of 1916, 
as Ludendorff acclimatised to conditions on the Western 
Front, did anything approaching mission command 
operate at intermediate and senior levels. Otherwise, it was 
the German High Command which not only dominated 
decision-making but also collated and sifted lessons learnt 
reports and generated and disseminated new doctrine. Any 
attempt on the part of subordinate formations to produce 
new best practice was stamped upon. As the situation 
deteriorated, command only grew yet more sclerotic, with 
ideas of delegated command evaporating. Ludendorff set 
2 Albrecht von Thaer, Generalstabsdienst an der Front und in der O.H.L. (Siegfried A. Kaehler, ed.), (Göttingen, Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1958), 
 
pp. 187-8
the tone. He was a notorious micro-manager. Quick to 
blame and slow to praise, he treated his subordinates 
with increasing disdain and aggression, eroding their 
confidence and initiative. This was partly a function 
of his personality. But also important was a command 
system rotten from the head down where the Chief of the 
General Staff owed his position entirely to the goodwill of 
a flaky Kaiser. The insecurity this generated transmitted 
itself down through the ranks of command and spread 
fear through an already inherently unstable structure.
This, in turn, contributed to the second reason: poor 
information flow. As the news got worse, after-action 
reports too often told the boss what he wanted, not 
what he needed, to hear. In particular, staff officers were 
unwilling to admit the weakness of the German army to 
Ludendorff.2 Consequently, inconvenient truths remained 
untold, objectivity fell away, and decisions were made on 
the basis of increasingly flawed information. Failure to 
analyse experience honestly led to the wrong problems 
being identified, the wrong lessons being learnt and the 
wrong solutions put forward.
A third factor was also at work. The German army, like 
most armies, was a ‘can-do’ institution which saw itself 
as able to solve problems. It identified, correctly, that 
its comparative advantage vis à vis the Allies lay at the 
tactical, rather than the operational or strategic levels of 
war.

A third factor was also at work. The German army, like 
most armies, was a ‘can-do’ institution which saw itself 
as able to solve problems. It identified, correctly, that 
its comparative advantage vis à vis the Allies lay at the 
tactical, rather than the operational or strategic levels of 
war. Germany could not hope to win a drawn-out war of 
economies and industries, but on the battlefield, German 
soldiers might be able to out-think and out-manoeuvre 
their enemies and offset enemy mass with agility. 
Consequently, the tactical level was where it concentrated 
its efforts. Even where tactical innovation seemed 
successful, as in the case of stormtroop tactics and the 
early gains made during the German offensives of spring 
1918, the failure to see that it was heading into a strategic 
blind alley cost Germany dearly. Seeking to address 
operational, and sometimes even strategic, problems with 
tactical solutions was doomed to failure. The strategic tide 
could not be turned by tactics alone. Tactical obsession 
meant that the Germans missed three salient facts: first, 
that they had already been defeated at the political and 
strategic levels of war; secondly, that their immediate 
problem was the operational one of matching allied 
tempo and resources; and, thirdly, that British tactical 
improvement had shifted the battlefield terms of trade 
against the German troops such that more was required 
than just ironing out their mistakes. When the disease was 
being misdiagnosed, there was little chance of a cure.

12 | The British Army Review 174: Winter 2019
This misconception of the army’s role and capacity led 
to two further tragedies. First, its confidence in its ability 
to solve problems outran its capability. This caused 
immense problems at the strategic level. If the German 
army hadn’t presented the Schlieffen Plan as a workable 
military solution to Germany’s political problems, after 
all, the war might never have started. Once war broke out 
and the Schlieffen Plan had failed, the high command 
continued to believe that it could find tactical answers to 
the impossible strategic situation Germany had created 
for herself, and so refused to consider any kind of climb-
down and negotiated peace (even had one been possible). 
Secondly, once war had begun, the Germans kept looking 
for tactical answers when it would have been better for all 
to accept the strategic logic of the situation. If there is a 
lesson for today, it is surely that the military needs to be 
ruthlessly honest, both with itself and with its political 
masters, about what it can and cannot achieve.
As for the British, some historians talk about how the 
British climbed ‘a learning curve’, and certainly the 
3 See Fox, Aimée, Learning to Fight: Military Innovation and Change in the British Army, 1914-1918 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 
 
2018)
British army had learnt, not only how to fight in new 
ways, but also how to learn. It evolved a process to 
capture lessons learned, distil the most important and 
revise best practice through new doctrine. Sometimes, 
the new approaches were codified and published in 
widely disseminated doctrine publications and taught 
in a wide variety of schools and courses on subjects 
from sniping to staff work. Sometimes, they were spread 
through the many informal channels of communication 
which linked the army within and between theatres 
scattered all over the world. 
The army managed to construct a highly flexible 
and effective system of learning systems, operating 
simultaneously down multiple different channels, each 
characterised by varying degrees of formality and 
central control, to ensure innovation and adaptation 
was as effective and efficient as possible.3 Whether 
this happened by design or fortunate accident remains 
unclear. What is certain, though, is that implementation 
remained extremely patchy: right up until the end of the

28th September 1918. © IWM (Q 9348)

war, for all the units and formations that did a good job 
of employing the latest methods, there were others which 
never got the hang of it. The BEF did not always either 
fully internalize or implement the lessons it had learnt. 
The efficiency with which information was disseminated 
varied widely and some units seem to have been unable 
to process new information sufficiently well to change 
their approach. The British Army of 1914-18 appears 
as a very imperfect learning organization incapable of 
generating uniform change in any systematic fashion, 
very haphazard next to the French and, especially, 
German armies, both of which employed a more 
centralised process within which the centre played a 
much more active role in promoting adaptation.

This, however, is to misunderstand the culture of the 
British army of the time, and to look through today’s 
spectacles at yesterday’s institution. Modern Anglo-
American military analysts have become accustomed 
to seeing innovation implemented in a centralised and 
process heavy way due to the very particular requirements 
of NATO interoperability, where innovation has often led 
by the (very large) US military, and where clarity and 
uniformity are essential if troops from many different 
countries are to work together in mutually predictable 
ways. While the British army of the First World War can 
seem amateurish by such standards, their application 
is somewhat inappropriate. The British army had a long 
tradition of laissez-faire. Pre-1914, within broad and 
generally accepted principles of war, it preferred to leave as 
much latitude as possible to commanding officers to train 
the men they would lead into action, rather than impose 
centrally devised programmes. 
The flexibility this engendered seemed better suited to 
the wide range of environments British soldiers were 
likely to find themselves operating in, all over the world, 
than the uniformity instilled in conscript armies almost 
exclusively designed to fight on the continent. This 
also fed into the way British officers tended to perceive 
themselves as pragmatists and skilled improvisers. In a 
distaste for theory and prescriptive rules they saw one of 
the features which set themselves apart from their French 
and German counterparts, who seemed in contrast keen 
Royal Aircraft Factory S.E.5 and S.E.5a biplanes of No. 29 Squadron RAF lined up ready to start a flight over enemy lines, 1918 © IWM (Q 60608)

14 | The British Army Review 174: Winter 2019
on abstract ideas, elaborate doctrine and programmatic 
solutions.4 Between 1914 and 1918 the BEF tended 
to allow more free play to the periphery than its allies 
or enemy and there were times, in 1918 at least, when 
operations became more mobile and the importance of 
synchronised fires shrank relative to that of manoeuvre, 
where this helped, rather than hindered, operations. As a 
result, the British proved an unpredictable opponent. The 
Germans, in contrast, were less so. Indeed, British ‘bite 
and hold’ tactics were designed precisely to chew up the 
German counter attacks which were bound to come in as 
soon as ground was lost.
We are confronted, therefore, with a contrast between two 
militaries with very different approaches to innovation 
and adaptation: the Germans centralised, programmatic 
and uniform, the British devolved, unsystematic and 
ad hoc. The British approach demonstrably won out. 
Just because that was the outcome on the Western 
Front in 1918 doesn’t mean that the organic, pragmatic 
British model is inherently better than the systematic 
German one in all contexts. Indeed, the example of the 
French army - the approach of which was much closer 
to that of the Germans than the British - suggests that 
programmatic approaches could work on the Western 
Front. In other words, it wasn’t the learning culture 
itself which was decisive, but something about how the 
institutions worked with those cultures.
The big difference is that the British clearly understood 
the laissez-faire spirit of their military and worked with 
the cultural grain, facilitating change and enhancing 
effectiveness even at the expense, sometimes, of 
uniformity. The German army, by contrast, thought it 
was flexible but actually wasn’t. Under pressure, the 
agility it believed it possessed became arthritis. The 
conflict between devolved authority and central control 
caused significant disruption to its attempts to change, 
with the drive for one-size-fits-all solutions undermining 
effectiveness. Knowing how to drive change, even 
revolutionary change, requires acute sensitivity to 
organisational culture: the British had it and the 
Germans didn’t. The lasting lesson of the First World 
War for modern militaries is not that they should fight 
in this way or that, but that they need to understand the 
culture within which they must work and create a culture 
that enables them to respond flexibly and creatively to 
the situations they find themselves in. 
There are, of course, three complicating factors: First, 
understanding the ethos of any organisation, even

make much sense to talk of a single culture even at the 
level of the single service. This is obviously the case 
for the British Army, with its distinct and very diverse 
regiments. Second, no individual can hope to effect much 
observable change during a 2 or 4-year posting: one must 
be prepared to play a much longer game and accept that 
results might not make themselves properly felt for a 
generation. Third, change might look relatively easy to 
effect in a crisis, such as the greatest war ever fought 
to date: it might appear much harder in peacetime. 
The pressure of war is a powerful inducement to reduce 
or remove constraints, radically shrink lead times or help 
override cultural barriers. But the cost is great.

A British soldier checks a wreck of a tram in the ruined Grande Place at Douai, 25 October 1918 © IWM (Q 11407)
In conclusion, the leadership of the British and 
German militaries faced these situations daily during 
the First World War. They dealt with them in very 
different ways, which played directly into the outcome 
of the war, with the British understanding three things 
better than the Germans. First the importance of force 
employment and learning. Secondly, the difficulty of 
learning. Thirdly, the importance of identifying what 
kind of change your organisation needs and can tolerate, 
and of working out how to use institutional culture to 
drive, shape and lead transformation. The British were 
not perfect at any of this, but they were better at it than 
their enemy, and that, after all, was all that was required.

teaches courses on conflict from Homer to Helmand. He

Prince Rupprecht and Germany's War on the Western

the Defeat of Germany in 1918 (Cambridge University

for the British Army Book of the Year award. He was

n October 2018, the British Army conducted its third 
and final Army Staff Ride as part of Operation Reflect. 
The German Bundeswehr had sent delegations to the 
staff rides in 2014 and 2016 and the German participants

the British invitation to participate in the last staff ride in 
2018 found a lot of open doors in the German Army, and, 
consequently, the German delegation sent to the 2018 
staff ride was the largest contingent that the Bundeswehr 
sent between 2014 and 2018 - in total 17 staff officers 
plus an administration team of one Captain and three 
Warrant Officers. 
The participants were chosen on three principles: 
They had to be volunteers, they had to have an interest 
in military history and they had to have the necessary 
language skills to participate in a meaningful way in the 
syndicate discussions. In order to prepare for the staff ride 
all participants were assembled at the German Armed 
Forces Centre for Military History and Social Sciences 
in Potsdam (ZMSBW) for three days in September. 
Every member of the delegation had to deliver a short 
presentation on matters ranging from the strategic context 
of 1918 down to tactical questions. This, together with 
further presentations by experts on the historical situation 
in 1918 and the current British Army of 2018 gave the 
participants a good grounding for the staff ride and the 
wider understanding of the British Army.

The staff ride followed the theme of ‘four armies in 
four days’. The first day was the ‘German day’ and the 
Bundeswehr oversaw the stands. In collaboration with 
the British Army, the delegation had prepared stand 
material and the staff ride participants were introduced 
by German officers (who were fully trained historians 
with PhDs) to the German tactical and operational 
concepts and the conduct of the Michael Offensive 
in March 1918. Prior to the staff ride, a German 
administration team had conducted a recce that had 
proved important for the design of the stands, but it 
would not have been possible to run the stands without 
the help of the British Royal Logistic Corps (RLC), which 
was exemplary throughout the staff ride. 
As always, it was the attention to detail that left the 
German delegation in admiration of the package that 
the British Army had put together: The different types 
of national food for the different days and the bugler 
who played national tunes did not go unnoticed! It has 
to be said that the rations of the ‘Allied days’ were more 
appreciated than those of the German day…not because 
of the taste, but merely because of the quantity. This 
added a sense of realism to the staff ride; there are 
numerous accounts from German units that stopped 
their offensive actions in the spring of 1918 because they 
were looting Allied supply depots. Luckily, our supply 
situation improved from day two onwards and we did not 
have to revert to such drastic measures! 
In addition to learning about the First World War and its 
relevance for today, the staff ride also gave the delegation 
the opportunity to reflect on the Bundeswehr’s approach 
to history and the commemoration of the war dead. 
The German participants were impressed by the way 
in which the other national delegations could discuss 
historical issues and bring their relevance to the 21st 
century. An open, frank and meaningful discussion of 
these topics is very difficult in Germany - the minefield of 
German history, in particular the dark years of the Third 
Reich - largely prevents such an approach. 
It was impressive to see how other armies talk about the 
First World War and include this conflict as an integral 
part of their military traditions. In Germany, the First 
World War is not officially part of the military tradition. 
The official Bundeswehr tradition rests on three pillars: 
The history of the German Wars of Liberation in the early 
19th century, the Stauffenberg plot of the 20th of July 1944 
to assassinate Hitler and the history of the Bundeswehr 
after the Second World War. A good example of the 
different perceptions could be seen during the combined 
British, French and German field service at the military 
cemetery at Vauxbuin: while the French and the British 
padres mainly spoke about the suffering of the First World 
War and the military personnel involved, the speech by 
the German military padre concentrated more on universal 
suffering in both wartime and peace - a fact that was 
noticed not only by the German delegation, but also 
the international contingent. Indeed, the remembrance

this experience on the German ‘national psyche’

Russia now not only sees the value in being militarily 
strong on paper, but is also willing to deploy part of this 
increasingly powerful military machine to not just protect, 
but advance, Russia’s national security interests. 
 
As in Part One, this part draws heavily on Gerasimov’s 
other published pronouncements, the bulk of which, as 
far as this author can tell, have not been examined when 
attempting to analyse Russia’s military actions on the

better understand the purpose of Russian military action

SPECIAL REPORT
M
edium Armour (MA) as a concept remains 
ambiguously defined and awkwardly employed.1 
Where the British Army has developed its approach for 
heavy and light armoured capability, the conceptual 
direction for MA has stagnated. Force structures, 
fiscal constraint, and the recent campaigns in Iraq and 
Afghanistan have all played their part in muddying the 
waters, to the extent that no clear vision exists as to 
what MA needs to be and therefore how it should be 
employed at the tactical level.

ction for MA has stagnated. Force structures, 
fiscal constraint, and the recent campaigns in Iraq and 
Afghanistan have all played their part in muddying the 
waters, to the extent that no clear vision exists as to 
what MA needs to be and therefore how it should be 
employed at the tactical level. This article will identify 
a historical precedent for the employment of tracked 
MA that has relevance for the future force, and from 
this analyse a set of key values that will inform the 
utility of the contemporary capability by answering 
two key questions: Can a set of values be identified 
that capture the essence of what MA needs to be, and 
the conditions within which its employment is best 
suited? Can these values, and subsequent lessons 
learnt from the historical precedent, inform a definition 
for the capability? These questions will be answered by 
exploring the tension which exists around some of the 
contemporary definitions for MA, before considering 
the capability’s genesis from the period of the interwar 
years up to the start of the Normandy campaign, 
June 1944. 
WHAT IS MA?
DEFINITIONS; CONFUSION AND AMBIGUITY
The term ‘Medium Armour’ is tarnished by the light of 
recent failed procurement programmes and a decade 
spent campaigning in Afghanistan where Protected 
Mobility Vehicles became the key unit for delivering a 
mobile, ground-based effect. Confusion and ambiguity 
reign supreme, with no single view representing what 
MA actually is. For example, in 2007 the House of 
Commons Defence Committee Report The Army’s 
requirement for armoured vehicles: the FRES programme… 
set out the requirement for a medium weight vehicle as a

Paper, Advanced Command and Staff Course, Number 18, Sep 14- Jul 15
2 House of Commons Defence Committee, ‘The Army’s requirement for armoured vehicles: the FRES programme: Government Response to the 
 
Committee’s Seventh Report of Session 2006-07’ (The Stationery Offi e 11 May 2007), 2
3 Ibid, p 5
4 Brooke-Holland, L., Modernising the Army’s armoured fighting vehicles’ House of Commons Briefing Paper, Number 08186 (11 April 2018): 15.
5 Skrmetta, Sean R., Major, ‘Fighting the Big War with the Small Hammer: Operational Planning for the Medium Force’ (School of Advanced 
 
Military Studies diss., US Army Command and General Staff College, Fort Leavenworth, Kansas 2015), 3-4.
direct response to the Snatch Land Rover’s vulnerability 
to roadside bombs in Iraq and Afghanistan.2 Likewise the 
report went on to cite the Ministry of Defence’s upwardly 
revised armour requirement for the failed Future Rapid 
Effects System programme, consequently increasing 
the weight from 17 tonnes to a maximum of 27 tonnes. 
Concluding ‘…we consider it vital that UK troops are 
provided with sufficient protection…’.3 A politicisation 
of the issue surrounding British troop casualties in 
these two theatres led to fixing design priorities that 
compromised the key principle of a medium weight 
capability; that of mobility.
By contrast, 11 years later the House of Commons 
Briefing Paper Modernising the Army’s armoured fighting 
vehicles, defined MA as ‘…weighing up to 45 tonnes 
but easier to deploy over large distances than heavy 
forces and offering a balance of firepower, protection 
and mobility’.4 
Finally, Major Sean Skrmetta in his paper Fighting the 
Big War with the Small Hammer: Operational Planning 
for the Medium Force focuses more on MA offering a 
down-scaling capability, as follows; ‘(The medium 
force can be defined as)…any force which reduces its 
capabilities to increase its operational and/or strategic 
reach.’5 This definition certainly tackles the hitherto 
lack of emphasis on strategic and operational mobility, 
however it suggests the force can only be scaled down 
and not up, constraining the commander in the level he 
can escalate to and predominantly basing all medium 
force capability at the lighter-end of the spectrum. 
In this respect, it is vital to understand the relationship 
between MA and the Medium Force. As with Skrmetta’s 
definition, the two are viewed as synonymous, however 
MA must be seen as a component of the Medium Force 
which allows the delivery of effects at the higher-end 
of the warfighting scale yet still retaining its 
operational mobility.

Another option, perhaps more pertinent to the current 
situation, has been to define the capability based on its 
physical weight. This is problematic for several reasons: 
Firstly; a definition based on a comparison with heavy 
and light forces means it can only exist in relation to 
these capabilities. This not only creates issues if the 
platform gains weight (does it then become heavy 
armour?) but also mentally shackles the commander to 
thinking based either on a heavy(-) or light(+) concept of 
employment.

and light forces means it can only exist in relation to 
these capabilities. This not only creates issues if the 
platform gains weight (does it then become heavy 
armour?) but also mentally shackles the commander to 
thinking based either on a heavy(-) or light(+) concept of 
employment. Conceptually MA must exist as a capability 
in itself, in the same way heavy and light armoured 
forces do, and regardless of the fact it could only ever 
practicably operate as part of a larger entity. The fact 
that the armoured platform is delivering a medium effect 
for the medium force is what makes it MA, not primarily 
how much it weighs. Secondly; physical weight offers no 
parity for historical or even future comparison. MA today 
weighs the same as heavy armour (Infantry Support 
tanks) from the Second World War, likewise given 
current trends MA of the future could weigh the same 
as heavy armour today. By using this as a definition it is 
therefore difficult to draw on lessons from the past, and 
will potentially create false lessons for the future. Thirdly; 
modern technology means the correlation between 
mobility, lethality, and survivability is no longer quite 
so clear-cut. The issue therefore rests in nomenclature 
6 Fuller, Machine Warfare, 188
alone, with the term ‘medium’ falsely channelling 
practitioners’ thoughts.
AN HISTORICAL CONTEXT
The genesis of MA must be considered to better 
understand this confusion. The following sections will 
examine the emergence of MA and the subsequent 
doctrinal and organisational challenges surrounding its 
employment throughout the Second World War.
THE EMERGENCE OF MA - DESIGN OR NECESSITY?
The interwar period saw massive turbulence across 
the societal, military, and political spectrum. The paths 
adopted by policy-makers at the end of the First World 
War were therefore in direct response to these turbulent 
conditions; shaping the tactics, equipment, and doctrine 
the Allies entered the Second World War with. British 
tank design traditionally focused on the infantry attack, 
and therefore prioritised survivability over mobility and 
lethality. By contrast, German designers had focused on 
the fast- moving attack, therefore basing their designs 
on fast-moving and highly mobile tanks which could 
out-perform the British equivalents.6 Until the Cruiser 
tank came into service, Britain had entered the Second 
World War with two main designs of tank; the lightly 
armoured ‘Iron Steeds’ and the heavy infantry support 
The rear tank in each would most likely be the Sherman Firefly. Photo: Wikimedia, Released

 BAR SPECIAL REPORT | 31
tanks. While confusion still existed in both armoured 
design and doctrine, the Cruiser tank was considered 
a main armour role and represented a change in 
direction towards a design that sought to blend mobility, 
survivability, and lethality. This idea would subsequently 
dominate tank design for the next half a century.7 
Assuming the emergence of the predominantly Sherman 
Independent Tank Brigades represented the first defining 
moment for an MA force, it’s debatable whether this 
moment arose because of carefully considered design, or 
whether by chance shaped by the prevailing conditions 
of the war. By contrast, German tank design can be 
viewed as a careful timeline of methodical research and 
development, based on previous years of conflict the 
Panzer MkV was the product of this.8 
7 Ibid, 145-148
8 Johnson, Grisson, Oliker, In The Middle of the Fight, 25
9 Buckley, British Armour in the Normandy Campaign, 140
10 Ibid, 15-16
By 1943 there was a general failure to reconcile the 
confused doctrine with the various types of tanks the 
British Army now operated. Montgomery, a proponent 
of the armoured spearhead, had recognised the need to 
refine the current doctrine by merging the Cruiser and 
Infantry Support capabilities, thereby creating a ‘one-
size-fits-all’ tank. The US Sherman provided the closest 
example of this ‘Capital Tank’ vision9 and, come June 
1944, this became the predominant tank within the 
Armoured Brigades10 with the Cromwell and Churchill 
‘filling the gaps’ as required.

DEFINING VALUES AND THE HISTORICAL PRECEDENT
Based on current UK doctrine, the following 
characteristics will be discussed in detail: Conceptual 
Understanding; Mobility; Versatility; Enemy Force 
Capability; Terrain; and Persistence (sustainment of 
the force). These values will then be analysed against 
Operation Goodwood.
Goodwood had ultimately been designed to enable 
a breakout from the near-deadlock which had now 
befallen the Allied advance and which threatened a 
return to a First World War style stalemate.11 The use of 
overwhelming strength to force a rupture in the German 
lines was therefore required to restore this mobility.

Designed to fix the bulk of the German Panzer divisions 
by drawing them into the Eastern (British) sector in and

A CONCEPTUAL UNDERSTANDING
To gain the most from MA commanders and planners 
must adopt a mentally versatile approach, understanding 
that MA cannot simply be employed in a manner akin 
to its heavier sibling, for to do so would make it a 
size surrogate for the heavier capability. Instead, MA 
represents a system within a much larger system, that of 
the medium force, and must be employed as such. 
The conceptual versatility which accompanies the 
employment of MA must first recognise the physical 
limitations of the platform and the thematic factors of its 
tactical environment before any operational aim can be set.
During Goodwood a disconnect existed between 
understanding these physical limitations, the thematic 
factors surrounding the tactical environment, and therefore 
the way MA should have been employed. Positive and 
negative implications ensued, for example: Montgomery 
demanded full appraisal of all activity throughout the 
Infantry and Sherman tanks wait to advance at the start of Operation 'Goodwood', 18 July 1944. A Sherman Firefly is in the foreground. © IWM (B 7513)

 BAR SPECIAL REPORT | 33
operation, thus allowing him to carefully synchronise his 
set-piece tactical effects. His use of these tactics, while 
playing to the strengths of MA by placing a high premium 
on movement and tempo, denied junior commanders
the level of freedom of action necessary for MA to best 
be employed at the tactical level. These constraints 
subsequently led to opportunities for exploitation, 
created by the ebb and flow of battle, being missed by 
the force. What should have been a force able to execute 
the inherently maneouvrist principles its capability 
represented, ended up being a force constrained by 
thought designed in a more traditional mindset.
Successful employment of MA infers an ability 
to accept risk - risk which seeks to maximise the 
opportunities of a versatile and mobile force, while 
avoiding the threats which would ultimately constrain 
it. However, Montgomery focused his tactical planning 
for Goodwood on three main principles12 which invert 
this premise: The avoidance of heavy casualties; the 
preservation of combat efficiency; and to make best use 
of materiel superiority. Assuming the first and second 
principles are largely synonymous, to categorically 
avoid these implies a low appetite for risk, especially 
when the character of the conflict (that of an existential 
fight against a heavier enemy) almost inevitably means 
casualties will be high and combat efficiency lost if 
opportunities are to be exploited.
By planning Goodwood as a set-piece battle Montgomery 
sought to adhere to his three principles by matching 
action, effect, and outcome, and therefore reducing 
the risk to his force. His operational technique was to 
‘…concentrate great strength at some selected place 
and hit the Germans a colossal crack…’.13 Inflicting 
maximum effect on the enemy using essentially 
autonomous means (the rolling barrage) was therefore 
key to avoiding friendly casualties, thus adhering to 
this first principle. The suppression and disruption 
this rolling barrage caused to the German defenders 
would then be exploited by the highly mobile forces of 
the armoured divisions, thus allowing the Allies to fully 
maximise their advantages in manoeuvre and mobility; 
overwhelming the German positions through their 
relentless tempo. However, John Buckley argues the 
operational techniques employed throughout Goodwood 
created several unintended consequences for the fighting 
force14, all of which neatly support the premise that MA

induced the completely opposite effect. An over-
confidence in the effects of the barrage meant overly-
ambitious objectives were set for the armoured divisions, 
subsequently becoming unachievable once this barrage 
had dried up and once its lack of effect realised.

MOBILITY
Mobility must be the golden-thread design principle for 
MA, with heavier or lighter forces offering comparatively 
less or more of it. Mobility enables versatility at the 
tactical, operational, and strategic levels; as Lieutenant 
Colonel Davies notes ‘Medium-weight force across the 
land environment is focussed on tactical actions which 
maximise on the rapid projection of combat power…’;15 
at the tactical level the mobility of MA allows it to cover 
significant distance in a short space of time. Good tactical 
mobility also compensates for areas of key weakness 
in MA, and enables high tempo at the operational level. 
MA therefore sacrifices survivability and lethality for 
enhanced mobility, however to ensure this is maintained 
compensation must be sought which can afford it the 
additional protection (and firepower) it would have 
otherwise lacked. During Goodwood this was met by 
the rolling barrage, designed to destroy as much of the 
German armour as possible to allow the Allied MA an 
unimpeded advance into enemy territory. The mobility 
of MA is also directly affected by the force structures 
it operates in. For example, when operating in its most 
likely structure (within a combined arms grouping) 
careful consideration must be given to the ‘mobility gap’; 
the physical difference in mobility between MA and the 
capabilities required to support it, most likely mechanised 
and armoured infantry. Major General GPB ‘Pip’ Roberts, 
commanding 11 Armoured Division and tasked to lead 
the attack for Goodwood, recognised the dangers in only 
having limited integral infantry support (one motorised 
infantry battalion). At the tactical level the plan for 
Goodwood featured very little armour/ infantry cooperation 
from the outset; Roberts recognised how crucial infantry 
support would be for his lead armoured units, providing 
the ability to deal with emerging battlefield problems 
thereby allowing the armour to maintain tempo in the 
advance, yet what limited infantry he had been given were 
allocated separate tasks16 and were mounted in vehicles 
unable to keep pace with the MA.

34 | The British Army Review 174: Winter 2019
The tactical mobility of MA and the operational tempo 
it creates is self-perpetual; mobility at the tactical 
level generates tempo at the operational level, which 
in turn allows the commander to adopt an inherently 
manoeuvrist approach, thus generating more tempo. 
Should mobility be constrained this cycle can easily be 
broken and the tempo threatened, resulting in mobility 
paralysis at the operational level. However, arguably 
the constant drive by Montgomery to maintain tempo 
induced many of the perceived failures of the action. 
For MA, achieving and maintaining tempo must not be 
to the detriment of the survivability of the force. Tempo 
must be seen not as an end within itself but as a means 
to achieving rhythm (rhythm can only be battle-winning 
if it’s based on tempo that’s quicker than that of the 
enemy force), therefore allowing a concert of effects to be 
maintained at speed and ensuring capabilities work in 
harmony with one another.
17 Development, Concepts and Doctrine Centre, UK Land Power, Joint Doctrine Publication 0-20, June 2017, 31
18 DCDC, UK Land Power, 11
VERSATILITY
The Joint Doctrine Publication UK Land Power describes 
versatility as ‘…underpinning the ability of a land force 
to perform many functions; it lies at the heart of land 
power’s broad strategic power. Land forces have inherent 
versatility because… (they have) the ability to conduct a 
wide range of military and non-military tasks’.17 MA is 
neither a heavy nor light capability, however must be able 
to provide an effect that can reach into both capability 
spaces. This ability provides the commander a range of 
opportunities for bringing about an effect, critical if an 
ill-defined capability is to have utility in the contemporary 
environment. At the tactical level this versatility is the 
ability to seize and hold ground; ‘the ability…enables the 
physical control of territory and signifies the highest levels 
of political commitment’.18 This remains the preserve of 
heavy armour, however the tracked armoured component 
within the medium force must be able to accomplish this 
against an enemy force likely to be heavier in strength.

of combination, terrain, and perceived enemy weakness to 
achieve effect without being compromised by its inherent 
vulnerabilities.

The solution it delivers must therefore look to the powers 
of combination, terrain, and perceived enemy weakness to 
achieve effect without being compromised by its inherent 
vulnerabilities. It is this need for MA to be augmented with 
supporting arms that gives it its versatility. For example, 
the materiel mass the Allies enjoyed throughout the 
Normandy Campaign meant this power of combination 
could be bought-out with sheer weight of tanks; to this 
end where conventional wisdom recognises MA as best 
employed with supporting infantry, the MA in the advance 
on Goodwood had only the rolling barrage to mitigate the 
threat posed by the heavier German forces.
The ability to seize and hold ground represents different 
ends of the spectrum for what MA must achieve. Seizing 
ground reaches firmly into the domain of its heavier 
stable-mates, while holding ground is the preserve of 
light forces. As tactical actions at either end of the effects 
scale it is precisely this spectrum of employment19 
which gives the capability its place on the battlefield; 
inherent versatility enabled by its tactical and operational 
mobility. As Davies writes ‘The classification ‘‘medium-
weight’’ has the sufficient leverage and flexibility to 
design a force, in line with national priorities, which 
can complement lighter forces, operate in isolation, or 
support heavier formations…’.20 
ENEMY FORCE CAPABILITY
The suitability of MA for an operation must be defined 
by the enemy’s capabilities. For example, the Allied 
Shermans and Cromwells fighting throughout Normandy 
operated at an enormous disadvantage to the German 
forces, whose tank crews generally enjoyed better 
survivability and lethality. However, Allied forces 
compensated for this short-coming with what Johnson, 
Grissom, and Oliker refer to as the ‘Sherman Dilemma’; 
doctrinal and organisational steps taken (to) mitigate the 
disadvantages MA faces when confronted by a heavier 
enemy. These include high quality combined arms 
tactics at the lowest level; the effective application of 
supporting firepower; and excellent all-round integrated 
training for crews and junior leaders.21 Therefore MA’s 
disadvantages, when facing competent heavier forces, 
can be mitigated by the power of combinations and 
quality of the force. Assumptions made about the nature 
of the threat facing the force will dictate what elements 
make up the combined arms, and in turn this will dictate 
how the MA is brought to bear. For example, the Allied 
19 Davies, The Spectrum of Employment, in Is medium-weight capability a quaint anachronism or the harbinger of a future force?
20 Ibid
21 Ibid, 154
22 Buckley, British Armour in the Normandy Campaign, 15-16
23 Davies, Lethality in Is medium-weight capability a quaint anachronism or the harbinger of a future force?
Independent Armoured Brigades included a Sherman 
Firefly in each troop. Fitted with the 17pdr main gun, the 
Sherman Firefly was an innovative attempt to combat 
the more heavily armoured Panthers and Tigers of the 
German forces;22 maximum lethality was achieved 
through harmonizing combined effects23 at Troop level.
With the German armour the focus of Montgomery’s offense 
it became critical for the Allied rolling barrage to have 
maximum effect, therefore allowing the MA to overcome 
the superior German forces. British and American bombers 
delivered an initial bombardment of 7,000 tons of high 
explosive to a depth of seven miles between the line of 
departure and the Bourguebus Ridge to destroy as many 
of the German defensive positions as possible, allowing 
advancing Allied forces to bypass all but the strongest 
of what remained. However, a misjudgement had been 
made both as to the strength of the German positions 
and as to the extent of their depth, allowing a significant 
proportion to remain combat effective. Recognising the 
enemy’s capability as a key impediment to Allied mobility, 
Montgomery had planned the barrage to be heavy enough 
to allow the MA to penetrate deep into the enemy’s territory 
unscathed, however in reality the barrage was insufficient 
to enable this.

TERRAIN
MA must look to capitalise on the nature of the terrain, 
and indeed avoid geographical areas where compromises 
in its design will be most exposed. When operating in 
open and rolling countryside with a wide field of view, 
MA can maximise its ability to deliver kinetic mobile 
effect however, where terrain is less permissive mobility 
can be restricted and MA’s advantage lost. For example, 
operating in the Normandy Bocage the Sherman was 
particularly vulnerable to short-range German anti-
tank weaponry.

ld of view, 
MA can maximise its ability to deliver kinetic mobile 
effect however, where terrain is less permissive mobility 
can be restricted and MA’s advantage lost. For example, 
operating in the Normandy Bocage the Sherman was 
particularly vulnerable to short-range German anti-
tank weaponry. In this instance its excellent mobility 
was nullified by the close nature of the terrain, which 
ultimately threatened to induce operational paralysis for 
the forces advancing through; an effect at the tactical 
level having operational and even strategic implications. 
By contrast, the Churchill Infantry Support tank had 
comparatively poor mobility however coped well in the 
Bocage; its heavier armour and lower gearing made 
it significantly more mobile than the Shermans and 
Cromwells when facing the prevalent German anti-tank 
(AT) threat.
To achieve the most from an MA capability the two key 
characteristics of the battlefield must be planned against; 
the going of the terrain and the sight lines it will afford.24 
Firstly, as with any tracked capability the nature of the 
terrain will dictate where MA can’t be employed, and the 
consideration of terrain as part of the defining values 
will influence where it can be employed, with different 
types of terrain offering different constraints. For example, 
the more permissive the terrain the greater the utility 
MA will have; complex and semi/non-permissive terrain 
such as mountains and dense urban areas offer the 
defenders a multitude of opportunities to level the odds. 
However, in other instances MA may be able to operate 
in terrain that would otherwise be impenetrable to heavily 
armoured platforms, and therefore may be the only option 
a commander has to deliver an armoured effect within a 
complex environment. Secondly, acquiring a target and 
avoiding being seen call for an assessment of fields of fire 
and observation.25 Retaining the initiative, maintaining 
the tempo, and playing to the capability’s prime strengths 
relies on being first to act. This can only be achieved 
if the enemy and/ or his intentions are identified first. 
Avoiding the enemy’s line of sight is also important 
if a force is to retain the initiative, particularly in the 
advance. For example, at the start of Goodwood German

policy operated by the advancing Allies, meant that the 
advancing armour bypassed German defensive positions 
at speed only for those positions to ambush the follow-on 
reserve squadrons. Numerous examples throughout the 
operation demonstrate the folly of the Allied approach; 
brought about by an over-confidence in the effectiveness 
of the rolling barrage to enable tempo.
THE ABILITY TO FIGHT AND WIN
The ability of the force to fight and win the battle is 
critical for any employment of MA. Joint Doctrine 
Publication UK Land Power notes ‘…underpinning all 
that our land forces do is the ability to fight and succeed 
in combat against our adversaries’.27 This critical 
consideration therefore ultimately influences the power 
of combination required to defeat the enemy force, 
combinations in which infantry must be viewed as an 
essential (supporting) component. The lead armoured 
forces in Goodwood had only one infantry brigade in 
support, therefore the threat to the German defenders 
was very much binary; assuming the preliminary barrage 
had been survived, once the wave of advancing armour 
had passed the well-concealed German defenders could 
conduct AT ambushes and fighting withdrawals with 
near impunity. The MA was exceptionally effective at 
taking the position, however, it could not tactically hold 
or consolidate operational gains without supporting 
capabilities. This must be seen a serious flaw in the 
force generation of the three armoured divisions that 
took part. With the launch of Operation Goodwood 
in the early hours of 18 July, by mid- morning it was 
clear the initial success of the advance was stalling as 
opposition stiffened. By 1030hrs the rolling barrage had 
ceased, having delivered 7,000 tons of munition over 
the seven-mile advance28, and the armour was now able 
to deploy in formations more suited to the fighting they 
would shortly encounter.

Repeated attempts throughout the morning to take the

but over. At a tactical level the ability to fight and win 
was fundamentally compromised by a fire plan which, 
operationally, had been designed to enable tempo 
unconstrained by the immobilising effect of enemy 
resistance. Quite simply, the MA had ended up battling 
dug-in German defensive positions without the critical 
force-multiplying effect afforded to it from supporting 
arms (artillery and infantry); the worst position for such 
a force to be employed.
MA can be used as an effective political tool, providing 
a nuanced and tailored force response in situations 
requiring political sensitivity. For example, the 
deployment of MA could demonstrate intent yet whilst 
remaining below the threshold of perceived escalation 
commensurate with that of heavier forces. The ability to 
fight and win must therefore exist as much in tactical 
action as it does in the political arena; providing choice 
and versatility to compliment a comprehensive, full 
spectrum approach which seeks to achieve resolution 
through leveraging all the levers of power.

PERSISTENCE
‘Persistence…(is) the capacity of land forces to extend 
their presence and endure in an area for long periods of 
time…’.29 Captain Basil Liddell-Hart explored models 
of highly mobile armoured forces operating at reach 
and penetrating deep behind enemy lines30, a theory 
only possible if forces operated with a model based 
on logistical self-sufficiency; akin to how MA would 
need to operate. To avoid losing tempo through over-
extending logistical resupply, operating in depth means 
any resupply plan must be robust enough to deal with 
high tempo in an inherently unpredictable environment, 
and where any resupply action is likely to be undertaken 
with just the support of those assets integral to the 
force. For example, the resource-rich status enjoyed by 
the Allies throughout the Normandy campaign could 
only be maximised with a robust logistical sustainment 
plan. By contrast, the German Army, who arguably held 
the technological edge over the Allies throughout the 
war, did not value their resupply methods to the same 
degree, the Allies therefore proving more capable at 
projecting and sustaining the force. Training crews to 
be self-sufficient up to troop level allows a significantly 
greater degree of versatility, where the force can look to 
exploit opportunities that would otherwise be denied to 
it. The notion of self-sufficiency must therefore be used to

engender resourcefulness at the lowest levels and relieve 
pressure on certain capabilities that exist only in limited 
numbers across the force. For example, if a tank crew were 
trained to administer life-supporting medical care this 
would have an immediate effect on that Troop’s mobility 
by allowing them to remain in the fight without having to 
organise a resource intensive casualty evacuation.
To conduct bold and aggressive action (and therefore gain 
or regain the initiative) the MA commander must first win 
the ‘battle of the build-up’. These considerations beg the 
question as to how expeditionary MA can be; for a small 
deployment in a semi-permissive environment then its 
feasible such a deployment could be achieved, however 
when employed in a non-permissive major combat 
operational environment MA, and indeed the medium 
force, would have to deploy as part of a larger entity.
In order to exploit its key advantage it is essential for 
MA to reduce its logistical footprint as much as possible, 
however this also has the potential to deliver failure if the 
force either cannot sustain itself or extends beyond the 
point it can be sustained by others.
CONCLUSION
By studying Operation Goodwood through the lens of 
contemporary MA, a set of key failings and values have 
been identified. Montgomery’s plan to achieve tempo had 
the effect of inhibiting the critical element to his advance; 
mobility.

CONCLUSION
By studying Operation Goodwood through the lens of 
contemporary MA, a set of key failings and values have 
been identified. Montgomery’s plan to achieve tempo had 
the effect of inhibiting the critical element to his advance; 
mobility. The premium placed on tempo was therefore to 
the detriment of achieving the more suitable end-state; 
that of rhythm.
Four key factors inhibited the mobility of Montgomery’s 
(medium) armour: Firstly; the rolling barrage created 
false confidence in what it could deliver, and constrained 
freedom of action for those forces in its wake particularly 
when it had reached its culmination point. Secondly; an 
overly-robust bypass policy, created by the relentless drive 
for tempo, led to core soldiering skills being forgotten and 
over-looked. Thirdly; a lack of support from combined 
arms. Not only were there not enough infantry to support 
the advance but in circumstances where they did operate 
with the MA they couldn’t keep up due to the unsuitability 
of the vehicles they were mounted in. Finally, a military 
mindset too focused tactically on recent armoured 
successes in other theatres, and operationally and 
strategically too couched in the set-piece actions that had 
dominated world conflict up until that point in time, meant 
the action was too constrained by obsolete thought.
Can a set of values be identified that capture the essence 
of what MA needs to be, and the conditions within which 
its employment is best suited?
Goodwood essentially featured a force based solely 
around an MA capability; with the resultant effect just as 
likely to have been suffered in a contemporary operating 
environment as in 1944, regardless of differences in 
weapon capabilities. Therefore, by studying the operation 
as a predominantly MA action elements can be identified 
that remain unaffected by time, and from which ‘timeless’ 
values can be drawn. These timeless defining values 
must all be considered when assessing whether MA is 
suitable for an operation, or indeed to what extent it

will be employed with its supporting capabilities and 
within the Medium Force. The utility of MA lies in its 
employment within a broad conceptual framework; one 
which embraces the complexity and diversity of the 
different types of operations a nation may call upon its 
force to execute31, and one which allows the commander 
the freedom of action to employ MA’s key strengths 
at the point it will have greatest effect. These values 
inherently recognise this broad spectrum and therefore 
seek to add clarity by providing the commander, at both 
a tactical and operational level, the necessary handrail 
to leverage the capability’s key strengths when planning 
for its employment. Mobility must remain at the heart of 
MA’s employment; where speed, agility, and shock action 
create versatility at all levels, enabling the commander 
to deploy the capability at reach and achieve operational 
fluidity by keeping an enemy force at bay until heavier 
follow-up forces arrive.
How can these values, and subsequent lessons learnt 
from the historical precedent, inform a definition for the 
capability? Not least for the reasons hitherto discussed, 
trying to define what MA is will always be problematic 
because of the broad spectrum of employment it must 
operate in. It is not an all-things- to-all-people force, but 
instead an armoured capability that can be scaled-up 
or scaled-down with supporting capabilities to deliver 
a tailored effect. Any definition must therefore cover 
two elements: Firstly; the core nature of MA (at its 
irreducible minimum what is it?), and secondly; its 
ability to be tailored. Both parts to this definition will 
now be summarised.
31 Johnson, Grisson, Oliker, In the Middle of the Fight, p 30
Definition part 1 As an irreducible minimum MA 
delivers a rapid armoured effect (speed, agility, shock 
action), ground-based manoeuvre and kinetic direct 
effect, all delivered at reach. Having rapid effect at the 
tactical level enables the commander fluidity at the 
operational level, and in turn strategic versatility. 
The term rapid effect is therefore central to this definition, 
whilst that effect itself is defined in part 2.
Definition part 2 The ability to deliver a tailored effect 
must be defined by what that effect needs to be; an 
effects-based definition which covers both the physical 
and conceptual. The central tenant must be based around 
the inherent tactical and operational mobility of the 
capability, considered in concert with the values already 
discussed.

Our fundamental task is like no other - it is to win in 
the un- forgiving crucible of ground combat. We must 
ensure the Army remains ready as the world’s premier 
combat force. Readiness for ground combat is - and will 
remain - the U.S. Army’s number one priority.1

T
he newly established ‘heel to toe’ rotation of Armored 
Brigade Combat Teams (ABCTs) to Europe in 
support of Operation Atlantic Resolve (OAR) provides an 
opportunity to demonstrate how the Army can reconcile 
deployment mission requirements with the demands of 
the Sustainable Readiness Model (SRM). The Army can 
optimize OAR deployments to this end by establishing 
enduring unit-to-unit partnerships between battalions in 
the rotational ABCTs and specific allies, and by directly 
linking unit readiness to the strategically important task 
of building interoperability. Rather than presiding over 
the atrophy of unit readiness as many past deployments 
have done, OAR is poised to return brigades and 
battalions to home station at a consistently higher level 
of combat proficiency and overall readiness than when 
they first arrived in theatre. If approached correctly, 
doing so will support the chief of staff of the Army’s top 
priority of maintaining readiness while simultaneously 
contributing in a meaningful way to NATO’s larger 
deterrence mission in Europe.
THE SUSTAINABLE READINESS MODEL: A CONTRACT
During the height of the Global War on Terrorism, the 
Army relied upon a model of tiered readiness called 
Army Force Generation (ARFORGEN). According to 
Army Regulation 525-29, ARFORGEN sought to provide 
a ‘sustained flow of trained and ready forces’ to support 
the regular cycle of twelve-to-fifteen-month deployments 
to Afghanistan and Iraq.2 Under this model, units 
would return from deployment and enter an extended 
period of reset, during which the formation conducted 
maintenance on its equipment while a large portion of its 
personnel departed for new duty assignments. The mass 
exodus of soldiers and leaders would temporarily leave 
the unit under-strength and untrained until sufficient

While in reset, units were designated as unavailable for 
rotational deployments or contingencies, allowing them 
time to build readiness progressively over a twelve-
month period. With as many as one third of U.S. brigade 
combat teams (the basic building block of American 
ground combat power) in reset and another third 
already committed to deployments primarily in Iraq and 
Afghanistan, the Army found itself extremely limited in 
its strategic flexibility.
However, the economic recession that began in 2008 
along with changes to the global security environment 
necessitated a new model for readiness. In a new 
atmosphere of diminishing funding and increased 
budgetary scrutiny, the SRM was born. The SRM seeks 
to increase the number of ground forces available for 
use by requiring commanders to maintain their combat 
readiness over time instead of allowing it to lapse during 
periods of rest. This is supposed to be done through a 
proactive approach to managing personnel, training, 
and maintenance. The stated objective of the SRM is to 
‘sustain over 66 percent of our aggregate regular Army 
units in a combat ready status at any moment in time.’3 
Doing so is intended to provide the U.S. government with 
greater strategic flexibility to respond to contingencies 
and thus better justify budget expenditures on ground 
combat forces. In this way, the SRM signifies a new 
‘contract’ between the Army and the American taxpayer, 
pledging a bigger ‘bang’ for every dollar spent.
Unfortunately, the pace of deployments has not lessened 
in recent years, and the fact remains that deployments 
often degrade readiness rather than build it. The combat 
proficiency of deployed ground forces tends to decrease 
with each passing month, as live-fire qualifications grow 
out of date, and opportunities to properly practice and 
evaluate key collective tasks are not always available. 
For example, battalions sometimes engage in advisory or 
capacity-building deployments that take the focus away 
from the units’ readiness regarding their core combat 
missions. Additionally, many locations to which units

find themselves deployed lack the training resources and 
facilities to support collective live-fire qualifications and 
large-scale maneuver training. These conditions risk 
imposing crippling readiness constraints upon Army 
formations as their skills atrophy before returning to

eight countries. The presence of this force ‘mark[ed] a 
significant moment in European defense and deterrence,’ 
according to General Curtis M. Scapparotti, then 
commander of U.S. European Command (EUCOM) and 
NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander.4 This deployment’s

CHALLENGES FOR READINESS AND INTEROPERABILITY
Currently, the U.S. Army has nine active-duty ABCTs 
with another being formed beginning in the summer 
of 2017 through the conversion of an infantry brigade 
at Fort Stewart, Georgia.6 These units are employed 
in a cycle of three standing, nine-month operational 
deployments through which these ABCTs currently 
rotate in Kuwait, South Korea, and Europe. However, 
this operational tempo, although predictable, quickly 
consumes the availability of these formations for other 
contingencies. At any one time, three of these ABCTs are 
deployed to these strategically important locations while 
another three are completing final preparations to replace 
those currently overseas. The remaining three have

Two of these rotational deployments are already well 
postured to support both the readiness of participating

The range facilities and vast training areas available

Similarly, in South Korea, there are also suitable ranges

only a single country with which U.S. ground forces 
must integrate, making interoperability requirements 
less problematic.

In Europe, however, U.S. forces face significantly more 
complex challenges in both optimizing the theatre’s 
ability to support the sustainable readiness of deployed 
ABCTs and in achieving the level of interoperability 
necessary for NATO’s larger strategic mission of 
deterrence. In terms of readiness, the most obvious 
challenge is the uneven level of training resources and 
facilities resident across the different NATO countries. 
In places such as Germany, there are robust ranges 
and training areas that can meet all the requirements 
of an ABCT. However, in other locations that lack such 
established resources, U.S. forces are unable to maintain 
training and live-fire qualifications at all necessary 
echelons. Though efforts are ongoing to improve 
ranges and facilities throughout theatre, this reality still 
endangers the SRM contract between the Army’s ABCTs 
deployed to Europe and the American taxpayer.
Less obvious to the outside observer are the challenges 
caused by a lack of sufficient time on the ground with 
specific partners to build true interoperability. Moving 
units around Europe, sometimes down to the company 
level or below, to participate in exercises of varying scale 
that reassure allies in a specific area of U.S. commitment, 
or to exercise the theatre’s ability to transport units from 
one location to another, are all laudable goals. However, 
there are significant drawbacks. In order to deter Russian 
aggression with limited forces, the commander of U.S. 
Army Europe declared that his task is ‘making 30,000 
troops look like 300,000.’7 Presumably, the repositioning 
of units across theatre is part of these efforts.
In practice, this ‘anywhere and everywhere’ approach 
to deterrence undermines interoperability efforts as 
deployed U.S. battalions seldom remain in one location 
long enough to make any real progress. Partnerships 
suffer as our allies quickly begin to see us as only short- 
term transients, as every new U.S. unit that arrives must 
start over from scratch with interoperability rather than 
building on a previously established foundation. Just as 
the soldiers and leaders on both sides begin to figure out 
how to operate together, the Americans load trains for 
movement to a different country.
Some might argue that this practice enables a force that 
can deploy anywhere in Europe and rapidly integrate with

any ally. Such arguments fail to consider the realities 
confronting units on the ground that would have to do 
the hard work of fighting alongside allies. Interoperability 
is difficult and messy work, even among nations that 
have highly capable, professional military forces who 
are motivated to work together for a common cause. 
At the lowest levels, junior officers and non-commissioned 
officers (NCOs) have to experiment on the ground with 
counterparts to identify and bridge capability gaps. 
This effort includes the development of common tactics, 
techniques, and procedures that can then be codified, 
practiced, and validated under realistic conditions down to 
the company, platoon, and squad levels.
To complicate matters further, unlike the situations in 
Kuwait and South Korea, U.S. forces deployed to Europe 
must deal with an alliance consisting of twenty-nine 
member countries, each of which speaks a different 
language and possesses sometimes vastly different 
equipment and capabilities. In order to provide a 
framework in overcoming these obstacles, NATO has 
divided interoperability into three components: technical, 
procedural, and human.
The technical component focuses on the compatibility 
of equipment. The procedural component, as the 
name suggests, entails a commonality of doctrine and 
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) as embodied in 
standardization agreements among NATO members.8 
Lastly, but certainly not least, the human component 
encompasses on the ground training that enables 
individual soldiers, leaders, and units to work together 
effectively during operations.
In an article published in May 2017, Lieutenant General 
Ben Hodges, the commander of U.S. Army Europe, rightly 
called on NATO members to acquire new and more 
advanced equipment to allow secure communications 
and to facilitate digital processing of indirect fires.

Unfortunately, there is little reason to believe that technical

across the Alliance in the foreseeable future. When 
one considers that in 2016 only six of the twenty-nine 
NATO countries actually committed at least 2 percent 
of their gross domestic product to national defense (and 
only five managed to do so in 2017), it seems unlikely

will soon occur.10 And, even if such purchases did 
transpire, more and better equipment is not the panacea 
for interoperability. Only deliberately planned combined 
training carried out over a sufficient period will ensure full 
allied integration.
One cannot wish away these difficulties, nor should one 
understate the impact of interoperability (or a lack there- 
of) on a strategy of deterrence.
WHAT CAN BE DONE
It is possible to optimize OAR to support simultaneously 
the readiness of rotational ABCTs and allied 
interoperability. Sustaining readiness allows the Army 
to fulfill its contract with the American taxpayer while 
achieving true interoperability keeps faith with our 
European allies by contributing meaningfully to NATO’s 
strategic mission of deterrence. The necessary steps 
begin with the establishment of enduring partnerships

consolidate at a nearby rail facility along with elements

MAKE READINESS EQUAL INTEROPERABILITY IN 
OPERATION ATLANTIC RESOLVE
The rotation of U.S. Army ABCTs to Europe in 
support of OAR offers an immense opportunity to 
demonstrate our ability to carry out a deployed mission 
while simultaneously meeting the obligations of the 
sustainable readiness contract with the American 
taxpayer. Enduring partnerships between U.S. units and 
specific allied countries optimize the ability to do so in 
the European theatre. Although challenges remain in 
some key areas, making unit readiness synonymous 
with interoperability in OAR is a worthy and feasible 
goal. It supports tactical integration among allies, 
operational flexibility across NATO, and a strategy 
of deterrence in the region. In today’s global security 
environment, when combined action among allies is 
likely to be the key to success in any contingency, an 
assessment of the readiness of U.S. forces must include 
an evaluation of their ability to integrate with those 
allies. Today, we talk about deterrence of aggression in 
Europe in terms of making thirty thousand American 
troops look like three hundred thousand.
Perhaps a better way to frame the problem is to think 
of deterrence as making that relatively small number of 
U.S. personnel the catalyst for developing a larger, fully 
integrated, much more formidable allied force that really 
is three hundred thousand. However, this requires U.S. 
ground units that are truly interoperable with our NATO 
allies. Enduring partnerships is a simple yet powerful 
way to achieve this end. 
Implementing these partnerships and synchronizing plans 
accordingly for combined exercises within OAR will take 
a significant amount of coordination and staff analysis at 
the highest levels across Europe. However, the payoff from 
these efforts will be immense for both the U.S. Army’s 
readiness objectives and for NATO’s deterrence mission. 
In short, the hard work is well worth the reward.

ar is often described in three levels; the strategic 
(the political), the operational (theatre level), and 
the tactical (the close fight). Each has a level of command 
and resources to achieve differing requirements. 
 
Operational art is defined as the directing and sequencing 
tactical actions towards a strategic aim. Field Marshall 
Viscount Slim was convinced that the division was the 
organisation to do this. The division, he argued, is ‘the 
smallest formation that is a complete orchestra of war’. 
The ‘full orchestra’ refers to an organisation capable of 
integrating combined arms (infantry, armour, engineers, 
artillery, signals, logistics, etc.) and executing operations. 
In more modern thinking, a former British Chief of the 
General Staff, General Sir Nicholas Carter, adds that 
a 2* headquarters has the right level of command and 
control wisdom to conduct the ‘orchestra’ because of the 
additional training and the experience of both its staff and 
its Commander.1 Critically, the division is seen as the first 
formation that can be employed to achieve an operational 
effect. Traditional doctrine suggests that a division will 
fight in the deep battle, resource the close fight and 
protect the rear of their operations. British doctrine 
wishes to reset the division as the lowest level in which 
operational ‘art’ can be practised and at which the Army 
will deploy. General Carter, stresses the ‘importance’ of 
the division but also calls for a reset in our understanding 
of what this means for hard power.2 The argument that 
the division is the first level of operational art is becoming 
set in British thinking.
The division should not be expected to conduct the ‘full 
orchestra’ of war. Like any military organisation, the 
battlespace it should consider is bounded by the range 
of its weapons and, in the modern division’s case, this is 
not beyond the scope of the tactical fight. British doctrine 
should follow a hybrid of the Soviet ‘tactical deep battle’

Over the course of the last 100 years the expectations 
of the divisional level of command have changed 
significantly. The idea that a division is the ‘full 
orchestra’ of operational impact has not always been firm 
in British military thinking. The emphasis of training in 
the First World War was at the division level as a tactical 
formation, the smallest formation which was considered 
effective.4 During the Second World War, divisional 
headquarters routinely only planned tactical activity for 
the following day. The Second World War division was 
faster at planning, and therefore executing, than today 
but arguably had a limited 24-hour tactical horizon. 
This tempo sometimes came at the cost of poor planning 
and mission failure with leaders who did not have time 
to plan effectively.5 The modern division can plan longer 
and more complex operations incorporating more assets 
but will take 36-48 hours to do so. This is significantly 
longer than the division of 70 years ago and slows 
operational tempo. Modern divisions also contain more 
vehicles and people meaning operations may take much 
longer to execute. The change in the role of the division 
over time is natural evolution, but one which is not 
necessarily helpful in understanding levels of warfare. 
The idea that the division has now become the currency 
of operational art has little evidence behind it. The only

The second aspect to consider is how to maximise 
success in combat. Jim Storr’s research into warfare 
identified that success is more likely with increased 
flexibility and tempo. ‘The bigger a force, the less mobile 
it is’ and therefore smaller sequenced actions are faster 
and more effective than slower deliberate ones.10 When 
analysing combat over 1942-1944, Storr concluded that 
divisions routinely only used a third of their combat 
power. During the first Gulf War, he identifies that 
brigades had combat force equal to a battle group that 
weren’t committed during most deliberate engagements. 
The Joint Force 2025 design is for one large division 
probably deployed inside a multinational corps. 
This is inherently inefficient and does not maximise 
combat power nor increase flexibility. Indeed, a British 
Army think tank concluded that the current divisional 
design could be defeated in a day.11 Storr’s research 
suggests that divisions can be smaller with limited 
impact on their military output if their activity is 
sequenced by a higher headquarters. With less resource 
a division is more effective but less suited to operational 
planning and must focus on fighting the close battle. 
Tempo is generated by smaller formations seeking 
surprise not larger, albeit more powerful, formations that 
are more vulnerable to enemy action.

A doctrinal alternative is the Soviet concept of the 
‘tactical deep battle’.12 There is a sense across the British 
Army that thought and doctrine is already restricted 
by a ‘rigid set’ of mental hoops that mean resources 
are dispersed and not concentrated for effect. The 
implication is that militaries are incapable of thinking 
outside of traditional formations.13 The Joint Force 2025 
plan for a three-brigade division suggests this is true. 
The resources available in 2025 do not adequately allow 
a division to have significant effect in the operational 
deep when focussed on immediate tactical objectives. 
Divisions are fixed to the ground they occupy and the 
range of their guns. Non-lethal effects will routinely 
take longer to achieve impact requiring more time 
and command stability than a manoeuverists fighting 
formation can offer. The doctrine of ‘tactical deep battle’ 
is a hybrid between the traditional western concept of 
close, deep, rear, adding a new space between the close 
and the deep. The deep should be considered as larger, 
operational goals with fewer links to the close battle. 
‘Tactical deep’ acknowledges that a division is simply not 
large enough to achieve a credible operational effect other 
than the defeat of a close enemy. It also conceptually 
frees capabilities such as information manoeuvre and 
cyber to focus on operational-strategic impact away from 
the immediate close battle. This is a more appropriate 
analysis of the equipment and capabilities that will be 
available to Joint Force 2025. It fits the ‘joint action’ model 
foreseen by the Ministry of Defence as a better model of 
future command.14 Especially considering the increasingly 
complex battle spaces that we seek to operate in. Strike 
brigades will find and enable armoured infantry brigades 
to fix and strike an opponent. Divisions must focus on 
excelling at fire and manoeuvre and enabling other effects 
but not necessarily commanding them.

AIR MOBILITY
Air mobility provides the ability to deploy, sustain and 
recover personnel and equipment, often over significant 
distance. At the operational and tactical levels, air 
mobility supports land operations, enabling manoeuvre 
when movement on land is difficult.31 During the Second 
World War Montgomery recognised the importance 
of this critical role and the need for sufficient aircraft 
to conduct it. He stated: No nation could afford to give 
to one Service the amount of air lift that Service would 
need at any particular peak moment in war. If the air lift 
organisation is to be an organic part of an army, it will 
cost more than if it was under the air forces; and the army 
will never have enough. In order to ensure integrated 
operations he believed ‘an air lift organisation must be 
dovetailed into air operations; you cannot separate an 
air transport system from air operations’, stressing the 
significance of this organisation prior to conflict to 
guarantee success once it commences. The shortage of

COMMUNICATIONS, COMMAND AND CONTROL (C3)
Frequent friction, and even conflict, has existed 
between what have become land and air components 
as each sought to establish their relative roles and 
precedence. To those that could see, the key to success 
lay in the integration of components to combine and 
maximise their strengths. Successful ALI operations 
depend upon command and control, which in turn 
depend upon communications.34 Montgomery and 
Coningham notably achieved this in 1943, integrating 
the efforts of their HQs as a prelude to turning the 
tide in North Africa. In many ways the simple truths 
were, and remain, obvious. Air power cannot take and 
hold ground; land power cannot match the reach and 
speed of air power. The lesson that army and air force 
operations must be integrated is one that has had to be 
learned and, on occasions painfully, re-learned.
On arrival in North Africa in mid-1941, Coningham 
assumed responsibility for a system where the RAF 
routinely failed to support the Army. Tedder directed 
he ‘get together’ with his Army counterpart. After 
the war Coningham reflected this was a decision of 
fundamental importance and had a direct bearing on the 
combined fighting of the two services until the end of the 
War. Cooperation of this kind, however, is not attained 
without effort; far more than rules and regulations, it 
requires time, willing, and persistence35 as well as mutual 
respect for each other's capabilities and limitations.36 
Personalities undoubtedly played their part in influencing 
and progressing this development in North Africa, but the 
underlying and constant imperative had been the reality 
of air power’s influence upon land warfare.
