CONCLUSION
CAS is often viewed as ‘the heart of integrated air 
power’. However, there are other missions across the 
air power roles that are as critical, if not more so, to 
land warfare. Control of the air is a requirement for all 
military operations. In the Gulf War it was achieved 
quickly and in full, setting favourable conditions for 
counter-land operations and a land offensive. 
In the Falklands War it was more limited, which saw 
Argentinean aircraft sink naval vessels that were 
directly supporting the land campaign. Although 
control of the air is often perceived as an independent 
air mission, land forces conducting special forces raids 
and integrating GBAD into the theatre air defence 
plan challenge this. Reconnaissance and battlefield 
photography were among the first air missions. 
As technology evolved, placing VDL receivers into 
soldiers’ hands, the unique perspective afforded 
by airborne ISR capabilities has greatly increased 
situational awareness on the ground facilitating more 
dynamic decision-making. In the absence of competing 
priorities for aircraft, CAS has played a significant 
role during COIN operations since 9/11. However, 
as experienced during Operation ANACONDA, CAS 
planning across an established, well-trained TACS must 
occur to ensure success during execution. Equally, 
attacking one’s enemy with AI prior the start of land 
operations, as in the Gulf War, can establish more 
advantageous force ratios for battle; in some cases AI is 
a more efficient use of air power than CAS. Air mobility

provides strategic, operational and tactical movement 
options to land forces. Heavy lift aircraft can move 
personnel, equipment and materiel from garrison to a 
theatre and, depending upon the threat, operationally 
within a theatre. Helicopters can, again depending upon 
the threat, move troops and supplies operationally and 
tactically within a theatre. The RAF’s lack of heavy 
lift aircraft reduced the deployment and sustainment

Effective ALI is essential to guarantee timely air support 
across all air power roles; it is not built upon the roles 
themselves but the C3 architecture established between 
components, requiring a mutual understanding and

or much of its seventy year history, Israel has been 
existentially threatened. Even today, aggressive state 
and non-state actors continue to deny Israel’s right to 
exist. Powerful adversaries seek nothing less than its 
outright annihilation. Across the region, the widespread 
perception of Zionist expansionism at the expense of the 
Palestinian people continues to fan the flames of hatred 
in a desperately unstable Middle East. For decades, 
the State of Israel, alongside the Occupied Territories1, 
has been the region’s pre-eminent crucible of terrorism, 
fomenting extremist ideologies and techniques that have 
ultimately been exported across the globe. 
Faced with this multitude of external and internal 
threats, Israel can reasonably claim to be on the strategic 
defensive, although operationally and tactically the 
Jewish state adopts an extremely aggressive and pre-
emptive security policy. It seeks to confront threats 
directly and forcefully when they emerge, rather than 
allow them to grow and present themselves powerfully 
at a later date. Simply put, Israel seeks to dynamically 
identify, deter, degrade and ultimately destroy the full 
spectrum of threats to its existence and wellbeing. 
For Israel, security equates to survival. 
However, Israel’s perspective of its own national security 
not only focuses on physical threats, but also on the 
threat of international political condemnation, which acts 
to degrade Israel’s legitimacy on the world stage and 
ultimately obstructs the completion of the Zionist project. 
In this regard, recent Israeli governments have placed 
large emphasis on the establishment of quasi-diplomatic 
relationships with regional Arab states, in order to quell 
spiteful rhetoric toward the Jewish nation, act as a 
bulwark against the growing Shia threat and attenuate 
the febrile diplomatic atmosphere within the international 
community regarding the future of the Palestinian people. 
THE PIVOTAL ROLE OF HISTORY AND GEOGRAPHY
Throughout history, the Jewish race has been 
brutally persecuted. For centuries, regular pogroms 
systematically targeted dispersed Jewish communities. 
The Nazi holocaust massacred over five million Jews,

The topography of Israel remains of fundamental 
importance to its national security. Israel’s internationally 
recognised borders, known as the ‘Green Line’, stem 
from the 1949 Armistice Agreement. Israel militarily 
expanded its borders in 1967 to include East Jerusalem, 
Golan Heights, West Bank, Sinai Peninsula and Gaza 
Strip. While Israel formally annexed the Golan Heights 
and East Jerusalem some years later3, it fully withdrew 
from the Sinai in 1982 and Gaza in 2005. However, Israel 
still controls international access to the Gaza Strip, in 
conjunction with the Egyptian government.
 
Although not formally annexed, Israel continues 
to occupy designated areas within the West Bank, 
including zones where Jewish communities have 
established ‘settlements’. The building of settlements 
has been driven by an ideological desire to expand 
across the entirety of the ancient Holy Land. Settlement 
construction has attracted vociferous international 
condemnation, including from the United States. 
Settlements also remain hugely controversial within 
Israel itself, with a significant percentage of mainstream 
Israeli society recognising settlement expansion as a step 
too far. However, aside from its importance to extreme 
Zionists, the occupation of the West Bank has more 
practical military underpinnings. The West Bank offers 
Israel much needed territorial ‘depth’. On the basis of 
the Green Line alone, Israel cannot reasonably defend

its territorial integrity, being only nine miles across at 
its narrowest point. A military thrust by an adversary 
launched from the West Bank could quickly reach the 
coast, cutting Israel in two. If Israel ceded the West Bank, 
the nation’s only international airport (Ben-Gurion) would 
be in range of mortars, rockets and shoulder launched 
surface-to-air missiles. Tel Aviv would be in artillery 
range. While Israel itself lies on a flat coastal plain, the 
West Bank forms a dominant mountainous plateau with 
a wide field of view over Israel to the West and the 
Jordan River Valley to the East. The latter represents 
the only natural line of defence against ground-based 
infiltration from Jordan. Furthermore, one third of Israel’s 
fresh water stems from a subterranean aquifer flowing 
underneath the West Bank: Israel is unlikely to cede 
control of this precious water source.
Similarly, the Golan Heights form the only defensive 
barrier to a ground-based attack from Syria, hence 
Israel’s occupation and subsequent annexation of this 
plateau. Militarily, occupation of the West Bank and 
Golan Heights represents the minimum required to 
provide Israel with sufficient defence in depth. In contrast, 
while the occupation of Gaza and Southern Lebanon 
provoked attacks by Hamas and Hezbollah respectively, 
the topography of both these areas offered no military 
advantage, hence Israel’s decision to withdraw from Gaza 
and Southern Lebanon in the early 2000s.

THE SHIA THREAT
Over the last twenty years there has been a marked 
shift in the security paradigm across the Middle East. 
The terrorist attacks of 9/11, the US invasion of Iraq 
and its subsequent withdrawal, the Arab Spring, the 
Syrian conflict, the rise and fall of the Islamic State, 
Russian encroachment and the Iranian JCPOA4 have 
all acted to change the security dynamics of the region. 
For Israel, the threats of decades past, emanating from 
Sunni Arab states and secular Palestinian groups, have 
largely waned. Instead, a newly empowered ‘Axis’ of 
Shia actors now poses the most direct threat to Israeli 
national security.

THE PALESTINIAN THREAT
Over the course of the last twenty years, the threat from 
Palestinian terrorist groups has diminished significantly. 
No longer do we see PLO, PFLP or Black September 
inspired hijackings of Israeli civilian airliners, or 
spectacular massacres of Israeli civilians on the beaches 
of Tel Aviv. The Oslo Accords of 1999 represented a 
paradigm shift in the relationship between the PLO and 
Israel. With the PLO, and its main political component, 
Fatah, finally recognising Israel’s right to exist, the 
Accords established a Palestinian Authority with civil 
jurisdiction over the Palestinian population.

ISRAEL’S DIPLOMATIC RAPPROCHEMENTS
For decades, the UN and its subordinate committees have 
been at the leading edge of international condemnation 
of Israel. Even a former Secretary General, Ban Ki Moon, 
opined that the UN had been ‘disproportionate’ in its 
criticism of Israel. Since its inception, over half the UN 
Human Rights Council’s resolutions have criticised 
Israel directly, leading the United States to describe the 
Council as having a ‘chronic anti-Israel bias’. The UN 
relief agency in Gaza has been independently accused of 
tacitly supporting Hamas. In 2012, the General Assembly 
granted the Palestinian Authority formal ‘observer’ status, 
allowing it to bring war crimes charges against Israel 
in the International Criminal Court. Thinly-resourced 
UN peacekeeping missions along Israel’s borders have 
proven to be abject failures.10 Only the steadfast backing 
of the United States, which continually exercises its veto, 
has prevented the Security Council from imposing other 
coercive measures on Israel, such as economic sanctions.
However, in order to mitigate the threat of international 
condemnation, Israel has become increasingly competent 
at forging bilateral relationships with other nation states, 
even in the face of historical antipathy and vociferous 
criticism regarding its activities in the Occupied 
Territories. As the security paradigm across the Middle 
East has evolved, Israel’s relationship with Sunni Arab 
states has improved markedly. Based on a realisation 
that a nuclear-armed Israel cannot be beaten militarily, 
Sunni states have increasingly found common cause with 
Israel in the face of growing Iranian Shia expansionism. 
In a practical sense, most Sunni Arab regimes are now

ISRAEL’S MILITARY AND SECURITY APPARATUS
Israel fields one of the most technologically advanced, 
ideologically-driven and well-trained militaries in the 
world: the Israeli Defence Force (IDF). However, with 
only 170,000 regular troops and 450,000 reserves, Israel 
cannot numerically outmatch its adversaries. Instead, 
Israel places a strategic emphasis on its ‘qualitative 
edge’. Specifically in the realms of armour, strike 
aircraft, missile defence, Special Forces and cyber, the 
IDF is lauded as being second-to-none. Conscription is 
mandatory for all, save for Israeli-Arabs and orthodox 
Jews. Israeli society has always retained a uniquely 
militaristic, ideological and nationalistic mind-set, with 
each Jewish citizen committing to serve the State of 
Israel and ensure its survival.
In parallel to the IDF, Israel’s state intelligence services, 
Mossad and Shin Bet, are also widely considered 
to be the best in the world. Mossad is tasked with 
identifying nascent external threats before they tangibly 
manifest themselves, a role which includes prosecuting 
Israel’s targeted assassination programme. This has 
resulted in the killing of 2,300 adversary commanders, 
operatives and scientists since Israel’s independence 
in 1948, although it remains a policy which is hugely 
controversial internationally.
Israel’s ultimate strategic deterrent is vested in its nuclear 
weapons capability. Although Israel has not openly 
declared itself a nuclear weapons state, preferring to 
adopt a policy of ‘deliberate ambiguity’, international 
governments estimate Israel possesses up to 400 nuclear 
warheads. Israel maintains a full ‘triad’ of nuclear 
delivery systems, including its Jericho III intercontinental

CONCLUSION
For decades, the State of Israel endured the very 
real possibility of being wiped off the map. While 
this outcome now seems remote, the Jewish nation 
continues to face-off against a multitude of powerful 
adversaries. Undoubtedly, the Shia theocracy of 
Iran now represents the most potent threat to Israel, 
augmented by a broad spectrum of ideologically-
driven Shia militant groups across the region, most 
notably Hezbollah. Israel’s responses to this threat 
are, as they always have been, pro-active, pre-emptive 
and aggressive. The range of strategic, operational 
and tactical levers employed by Israel remains diverse 
and complementary, including airstrikes against 
Iranian weapon transfers in Syria, assassinations of 
Hezbollah military commanders, cyber-attacks against 
Iranian nuclear facilities, conventional deterrence 
along the Golan Heights, forging of quasi-diplomatic 
alliances with Sunni Arab states and covert retention 
of the ultimate coercive measure: a nuclear weapons 
capability. In parallel, Israel continues its punitive 
measures against Hamas in the Gaza Strip and 
its occupation of the West Bank, while fending off

regarding the final status of the Occupied Territories.
The British Army can learn much from the Israeli 
experience. In an era where the United Kingdom is 
facing a return to great power competition, it would be 
wise for the British Army to engage pro-actively with its 
Israeli counterparts, across the full spectrum of military 
capabilities. Given recent Israeli experiences in Gaza, 
the West Bank, Lebanon and now further afield, vital 
lessons could be learned. In particular, the British Army 
could exploit the Israeli experience and ‘qualitative 
edge’ in terms of targeting, armoured manoeuvre, long-
range precision fires, air defence, tunnel warfare, urban 
operations, intelligence collection and the integration 
of women into combat roles. The Israeli Defence Force 
remains unequivocally world class in these areas: as the 
British Army, we should listen and learn.

from the integration of 4 YORKS Army Reserve soldiers within 2 
YORKS Companies during their deployment on Op TORAL 5 focusing 
primarily on the actions of Corunna Company, 2 YORKS as the author

A
s the Army Reserve continues to grow in line with Op 
FORTIFY objectives, it is more important than ever to 
ensure that the Army Reserve is employed appropriately 
and to greatest effect. Once a decision to mobilise 
reservists for operations is made, it is imperative that they 
are successfully integrated with their regular counterparts.
Employment of the Territorial Army (TA) was 
instrumental in the Allied success during the Second 
World War. Much like the Regular Army, the TA/Reserve 
Force strength has always surged in times of need. 
In 1939 it was announced that the TA would grow to 
a total strength of 440,000. Volunteer soldiers have 
historically displayed an ability to integrate seamlessly 
into a whole force (Regular and Reserve), enduring the 
same hardship and displaying the same tenacity as 
the Regular Army. Testament to this is that on D-Day, 
June 6th, 1944, the only Victoria Cross recipient was a 
volunteer. WO2 Stanley Hollis of the 6th Battalion, Green 
Howards was awarded the VC for his actions in single-
handedly storming an enemy pillbox.
Operation TORAL 5 saw 2 YORKS deploy to Afghanistan 
with 13 reservists from 4 YORKS (including the Padre) 
and 42 individual augmentees (IA’s). The Battlegroup 
was employed as the Kabul Protection Unit (KPU) where 
two primary responsibilities existed: Force Protection and 
Incident Response. Each of these tasks required attached 
reservists to possess soldiering skills entirely on par 
with the soldiers of the Regular unit. A determined and 
persistent insurgent threat would not make allowance 
for the reduced training exposure of a reservist. Whilst 
the attached Reservists would complete Mission Specific 
Training within 2 YORKS, they could not realistically 
also be present for the full Collective Training 1-4 (CT 
1-4) training package provided by the likes of Exercise 
WESSEX STORM. 
SETTING THE CONDITIONS
Combating any negative preconceptions of the Army 
Reserve that may exist within the receiving unit is crucial 
to successful integration. It cannot be ignored that there 
is an element of unconscious bias in the mind of some 
regular Infantry soldiers towards Army Reservists. Proud 
of their profession, they may be dubious that a similar 
output can be achieved by anyone other than ‘full-time’ 
Infanteers. For this reason, 2 YORKS soldiers were 
delivered a brief on the Army Reserve explaining the

EARLY CORRESPONDENCE
Once individual reservists have been allocated to sub-
units, early correspondence between the company and 
the soldier is beneficial. In this case an email was sent to 
each soldier by the OC welcoming them to the Company 
and introducing key personalities. This correspondence 
was intended to reassure the reservists they were 
welcome within their new sub-unit and that they had 
been considered on a personal level. The OC and CSM 
personally received reservist soldiers upon their arrival 
at the Unit, further demonstrating a genuine interest. 
Letters were also sent by the OC to the soldiers’ Next of 
Kin, explaining the deployment and their mission 
in Afghanistan.
TREATMENT AS EQUALS
From their arrival, the reservists were treated equally 
within the regular sub-units. Whilst an element of 
‘mentoring’ was required to bring them fully in line 
with their regular counterparts, they quickly became 
indistinguishable in appearance and ability. OCs 
conducted interviews with each reservist exactly as they 
did for their regular soldiers. A conscious effort was made 
to make them feel part of the sub-unit. 2 YORKS were 
fortunate in receiving their reservists relatively early in the 
pre-deployment process(4-5 months prior to deployment). 
This prolonged interaction, particularly throughout 
Mission Specific Training (MST), further aided integration.
After a short ‘bedding in’ period, the reservists we 
received became indistinguishable from our regular 
soldiers. They did exactly the same job, to exactly the 
same standard. You couldn’t tell them apart.1

80 | The British Army Review 174: Winter 2019
ENCOURAGE SOCIAL INTERACTION
2 YORKS’ soldiers welcomed the reservists into their 
peer groups and interacted with them socially as well 
as professionally. A company social event after the 
Mission Rehearsal Exercise (MRX) was an excellent 
opportunity to cement those bonds and new friendships 
prior to operations. 
BREAK THEM UP (TO AN EXTENT)
The 13 reservists from 4 YORKS mobilised for Op TORAL 
were broken down across 3 separate locations throughout 
Kabul. By splitting them up they could be effectively 
mentored by their regular counterparts, enabling effective 
integration and adopting their Modus Operandi. 
This approach was deemed favourable, on this occasion, 
over deploying them as formed sections. By breaking 
them down in to small groups of 3-5, they still had the 
support and familiarity of their fellow reservists but were 
better placed to interact with members of the regular unit. 
Formed sections may have presented an opportunity for 
segregation and a ‘them and us’ divide. That is, however, 
not to say there is no merit in deploying formed reservist 
sections/platoons when the requirement arises.
UPDATE THE PARENT UNIT
Periodic feedback from the regular unit to the reserve unit 
is important in keeping the reserve Chain of Command 
abreast of developments. Regular updates were sent, 
informing the reserve unit of their soldiers’ progress and 
their developing aspirations. Several individuals were 
identified as having the potential to attend JNCO cadres 
or officer selection in the near future. Such information is 
valuable as it can be acted upon quickly once the soldier 
returns to his parent unit.
DRIVING QUALIFICATIONS
The reservists deploying on Op TORAL did so as generic 
Infantry personnel and therefore no need had been 
identified for them to achieve driving qualifications. 
Understandably, it is often not feasible, due to civilian 
employment commitments, for reservists to arrive with 
specific vehicle platform driving qualifications; however, 
it certainly would make these soldiers even more versatile 
if driving qualifications could be attained prior to 
mobilisation as it would provide the unit with reservists 
capable of fulfilling multiple roles. Consideration should 
be given to qualifying reservists, where possible, for an

Units should ensure they utilise the broad range of

DE-MOBILISATION 
Prior to de-mobilisation it is important that each soldier 
receives an Operational Insert to complement their 
Annual Report. It is beneficial to combine this with a 
closing interview and a letter of thanks from the OC. 
The OC may also choose to write to the reserve unit 
CO thanking him/her for the contribution of troops and 
appraising them of the reserve soldiers’ performance on 
operations.
POSITIVE OUTFLOW
An operational deployment may serve as an 
advertisement for the Regular Army to some reservists 
and this should be capitalised upon before it fades. 
In the case of this deployment, one soldier who decided 
he enjoyed the Regular Army lifestyle, but was too old 
to transfer to the Regular Army, instead took up an Full 
Time Reserve Service (FTRS) contract at 2 YORKS.
SUMMARY
In conclusion, the integration of reservists within a 
regular unit on operations can be greatly enhanced. 
By giving personal consideration to the individual 
soldiers and making them feel welcome, whilst at the 
same time dispelling any negative attitudes held by the 
regular unit, one can best set the conditions for a smooth 
and successful integration.

Will Technology Provide 
the Solutions we Need?
Edward Faulkner, Full Time (External Placement (Academic), British 
Army), analyses contemporary British military concepts that favour 
technological solutions and draws lessons from the inherent flaws in 
the Revolution in Military Affairs (RMA). 
Pictured is a remotely piloted unmanned aerial vehicle (RPAS) being tested as part of the UK Governments Project MINERVA. 
MOD Photographer, Crown Copyright.

 BAR ARTICLES | 85
I
n 1930, the then Brigadier Archibald Wavell, wrote a 
piece for RUSI entitled The Army and the Prophets. 
In this article he examined the latest ideas from the 
eminent military theorists of the day - the so-called 
prophets - to propose which developments in military 
affairs had the ability to change the character of future 
war. Many of his predictions, such as his suggestion that 
the decision to restrict the military strength of the German 
Army in the aftermath of the First World War would foster 
a military organisation more readily adaptable to the needs 
of future mechanised warfare, are remarkably prescient. 
Yet an underlying weakness of the article is a tendency to 
overstate the role new technologies will play in the future. 
The fascination with technology is symptomatic of a wider 
assumption that the greater material capability a military 
has, the more powerful it will be. Contemporary British 
military concepts risk falling into the same trap. 
THE PROBLEM WITH POWER
Equating military capability with power is problematic.

THE PROBLEM WITH POWER
Equating military capability with power is problematic. 
For instance, it cannot explain why the British military 
failed in Suez in 1956 and why US forces were defeated 
in Vietnam. The weakness in such a simplistic 
interpretation of power lies in not exploring the relational 
perception of power itself. In his 1993 analysis of power, 
Stefano Guzzini provides a scenario to illustrate this idea:
The sanction of killing and the visible means for 
realizing it generally provide a powerful threat. Yet, if 
the threatened person is preparing to commit suicide, 
or does not value life so highly, the coercive capacity of 
the threat is reduced accordingly.1
So, power is not a fixed concept as ‘people act toward 
objects, including other actors, on the basis of the 
meanings that the objects have for them’.2 Thus, Russian 
military capability has different meanings for Canada 
and Cuba. A prominent critic of rationalism, Ned Lebow, 
uses the analogy of the status of Winkte in Sioux warrior

referred to as Winkte and were pushed to the peripheries 
of the community but over time the Winkte were often 
venerated for their mystical powers.3 In other words, 
power and status does not derive solely from becoming 
the strongest militarily; for example, Switzerland 
maintains its influence in the international system 
through affirming its credentials as a peaceable and 
neutral nation. Military power cannot simply be defined 
by military capability.
THE VAMPIRE FALLACY
Yet, conceptions of power defined by capability 
continue to manifest in military conceptual thought in 
the form of an acute fascination with the advantage new 
technologies can bring. General H.R. McMaster referred 
to this as the ‘vampire fallacy’ because the attraction is 
almost impossible to kill. The fallacy lies in focussing 
on advances in technology rather than the human 
aspects of war.4 The Third Offset Strategy, a US military 
concept still in refinement, stresses ‘the importance 
of technology and innovation for defence success’.5 
Meanwhile, Development, Concepts and Doctrine 
Centre’s (DCDC’s) Global Strategic Trends - 
Out to 2045 (GST45) goes as far as stating that 
advances in technology could alter the very nature of 
conflict.6 A tell-tale hint of the relationship between 
technology and concepts in the British Army, is the 
positioning of the team responsible for Conceptual Force 
(Land) 2035 (CF(L)35) within the Capability rather than 
Strategy Directorate. A senior officer in the Strategy 
Directorate admits that ‘technology has been a massive 
driver’ in the development of CF(L)35.7 
However, commentators such as Hew Strachan argue 
that ‘the strategic contours of war...have not been as 
decisively shaped by technology as our own belief in 
the remorselessness and acceleration of innovation

One key aspect overlooked by theorists who focus 
on technology, is the possibility that adversaries will 
develop their own technologies to counter the threat. 
Writing in 1945, General John Fuller, referred to this as 
the ‘constant tactical factor’ warning commanders not to 
‘suppose the ingenuity that led to the technology is not 
matched by an equal ability to find the tactical solution, 
or vice versa’.15 In the Future Force Concept (FFC) exciting

However, hard-won experience in Iraq and Afghanistan 
showed time and again ‘how cheap, low-tech weapons 
were able to counter expensive, high-technology US and 
allied systems’.17 These campaigns also highlight how 
considerations of political, historical and social issues 
led to a deliberate limitation of technology that would 
have otherwise provided a qualitative edge. For instance, 
the British Army did not deploy main battle tanks and 
severely limited the use of artillery in Afghanistan for fear 
of alienating the local population.18 
Over-dependence on technology could prove to be a future 
military’s greatest weakness. FFC identifies advanced 
command and control communications systems as a 
significant point of fragility19 because the reliance of these 
systems on the electro-magnetic spectrum leaves them 
vulnerable to attack. This weakness has been recognised 
by other militaries; for instance, the Chinese regularly 
train without electronic command and control sytems and 
the US Navy has reinstated astronomical navigation for 
their navigators.20 Another danger is the trend towards 
procuring costly new equipment at the expense of 
maintaining mass in the belief technological superiority 
will make up for inadequacies in numbers. This is an 
issue often raised in relation to the particularly expensive 
platforms the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force are required 
to operate. A House of Lords briefing uses the example of 
how a new destroyer might have the firepower of two older 
ones, but it also cannot be in two places at once.21 From a 
British Army perspective, CF(L)35 clarifies its attitude by 
stating that it prejudices mass for effect22; in other words, 
less soldiers and equipment but with more firepower.

LESSONS FROM REVOLUTION IN MILITARY 
AFFAIRS (RMA)
The false promise of RMA, which gained favour in US 
and Western military thought in the 1990s, provides a 
cautionary tale for future concepts. RMA relied on the 
premise that superiority in technology could make up 
for deficiencies in manpower and used the example of 
the First Gulf War as proof. It encapsulated a vision of 
clinical land campaigns where command and control 
of an adversary could be precisely targeted thereby
dislocating an adversary to such an extent that land 
forces need only ‘mop up’ final pockets of resistance. 
This was supported by intoxicating language such 
as ‘shock and awe’ and ‘surgical strikes’. The danger, 
though, is we fail to fight the war as it is, but as we

capabilities would have less utility’.25 For instance, the 
abstract way it was described meant it did not properly 
address the issue of fighting in built up areas. It was also 
geared to a very specific form of regular warfare that did 
not account for how the enemy would likely respond. 
The striking similarities between RMA and CF(L)35 
should encourage a more robust critique of contemporary 
British military conceptual thought. Sucked in to the 
hype, an adversary’s ability to similarly transform or 
adapt to meet the threat is ignored. At the 2018 RUSI 
Land Warfare Conference, it took until the second day 
of the two-day conference for an audience member to 
point out that the speakers seemed so preoccupied with 
discussing new developments in their own militaries 
that they had neglected any mention of the enemy.26 
In CF(L)35, the trade-off of mass and protection for 
firepower and mobility are likely points of weakness 
an adversary might seek to exploit.27 For instance, the 
complex geographic and human terrain of the urban 
environment, well-known for requiring increased 
protection and infantry mass, could be a battlefield of 
choice for an adversary lacking similar capabilities.28

meticulous account of the failure of the Royal Navy

of war - for ‘the harsh lessons of combat will always

32 Thornton, Rod, (2015) ‘The changing nature of modern warfare’, Royal United Services Institute Journal, 160(4), 40.
virtual environment is very different from reality and 
cannot simulate the real frictions of war that play on 
a commander’s mind. In the virtual experimentation, 
commanders are intuitively more likely to take greater 
risks knowing there are no repercussions if mistakes are 
made. Indeed, they are positively encouraged to seek to 
fight differently. Yet, this does not replicate the realities 
of the battlefield. In The Utility of Force, General Rupert 
Smith, the commander of 1st (UK) Division during the 
First Gulf War, recounts the weight of responsibility that 
influenced his decisions: ‘I felt these pressures palpably. 
I had all the up-to-date tanks in the British Army, and 
because the engines were unreliable I was given very 
nearly every tank engine in the inventory’.31 This begs 
the question whether a commander of a CF(L)35 force 
would not feel the same pressures even if it was largely 
RAS he or she was risking.
CONCLUSION
Military capability is regularly equated with technology 
in British military conceptual literature; the more 
advanced the system employed, the greater the combat 
power of the force. The hazard of applying this notion 
when predicting the future battlefield environment is that 
it leaves too much unsaid. The risk is that conceptual 
thought will succumb to ‘Maginot Line thinking’32; the 
French Maginot Line of the 1930s was symptomatic of 
fixed ideas on what the future threat was, how it was to 
be opposed and overly relied on technology to provide 
the solution. The French thought they had set a trap for a 
future German onslaught, instead they set a debilitating 
cognitive trap for themselves.

There has no doubt been some tangible success in 
achieving a CT4 award, but the Army is now in the 
midst of re-mastering the basics as part of the battle 
craft syllabus agenda. 
However, the argument here is that ‘training must 
permit failure; mistakes made in good faith….are to 
be encouraged where they enhance training’1 and it is 
based on my - and my team’s - observations on eight 
armoured, armoured infantry and combat service support 
BGs, as well as two armoured cavalry BGs conducting 
STRIKE experimentation, over the 2016 and 2017 
training seasons. BATUS has observed BGs succeed 
and fail missions in almost equal measure. Indeed, the 
latter has mostly produced a marked response and led 
to subsequent mission success. So there is a twofold 
aim here: describe the environment where BGs are safe 
to fail and how this can create a much better learning 
environment; and then make observations about how this 
culture could be exported across the wider Army.
DEALING WITH MISSION FAILURE
Success is stumbling from failure to failure with no loss 
of enthusiasm.
Winston Churchill
As humans, and in this context, men of arms, we 
don’t enjoy getting punched in the face. When we do 
experience this, we get angry and respond in kind. 
Misfortune and failure can illicit overwhelmingly 
positive responses, if we engender the right attitude 
and approach. When facing failure, as commanders and 
leaders, our emotional and physical reaction to it, in front 
of subordinates, is just as important as the actions we 
take to correct our shortcomings.
The After-Action Review (AAR) process provides the 
forum in which performance can be discussed and 
evaluated. It is backed by credible data, instrumentation, 
media and objective observations. 
1 GOC 3 UK Div’s Guidance, 22 Jan 2018
BATUS has continued the shift towards audience-led AARs: 
commanders at all levels have to break the bad news to 
their teams before discussing the way forward. Beginning 
this process of self-reflection by proffering explanations 
instead of excuses always leads to a more favourable 
outcome. ‘Owning’ mistakes and being receptive to 
feedback, exudes confidence, accountability and integrity. 
Without doubt, being resentful to criticism - however 
contested it might be - is a significant block to progress, 
improvement and ultimately subsequent success.
As experienced tactical commanders and leaders, we 
should all know what good looks like. Therefore we can 
offer up our own solutions to put things right. We know 
we can’t please everyone all the time and we can’t fix 
everything all at once. Action plans on how to - moreover 
on who will - fix things are most successful when 
framed against immediate (next mission), medium term 
(by ENDEX) and longer term (for subsequent training 
events) timelines. The fact that not everything can be 
immediately fixed underlines the fact that collective 
training events must be seen as a training process rather 
than a pass/fail training event in itself. 
Properly recording these plans to fix things is an equally 
crucial step. Noting down the key actions to prevent 
similar mistakes and failings is crucial. Taking a photo 
of this is a useful review after subsequent missions to 
identify where gains and improvements have been made. 
Not only does this provide an audit trail to any changes 
made, but the fact issues are being addressed instils 
confidence in subordinates that their commanders are 
taking proactive steps to avoid similar mistakes. These 
are just several short examples of the shift in culture we 
are striving for in BATUS, but how can this be expanded 
across the rest of our training process?
CHANGING ATTITUDES
War makes extremely heavy demands on the soldier’s 
strength and nerves. For this reason, make heavy 
demands on your men in peacetime exercises.
Field Marshall Erwin Rommel
At the root of the inefficiencies with our collective 
training process is the perception that mission failure is 

92 | The British Army Review 174: Winter 2019
wedded to career and MS implications. We must begin 
to divorce a perceived ‘failing’ of a collective training 
event from career and promotion prospects. Whilst I can 
extol the benefits of how we corporately learn more from 
failure than success, we have yet to see a complete and 
definitive split between failure and MS implications. 
Not only does this hinder constructive gains and marked 
improvements as described earlier, but the fear of failure 
actually does more harm than good. It perpetuates 
perverse behaviours: cheating, ‘fighting the white’, 
making excuses over offering explanations, disowning 
mistakes and disputing data.
This raises issues on several levels. Ultimately the 
conditions are set for people to put personal career 
aspirations ahead of actually achieving increased 
collective competence for their people.

The learning process at the US NTC is unquestionable, 
flowing from AARs all the way to COs writing letters 
of condolence to bereaved families in order to get their 
troops regenerated. The training process is calibrated 
towards answering the questions of ‘what did you 
learn?’ rather than ‘did you pass or fail?’ a question set 
that we should be bold enough to embrace. This could 
be backed by acknowledging that not only are lessons 
learnt, but the training event really tests and proves the 
commanders’ resilience and mental strength, and their 
emotional intelligence. Indeed, the training value alone 
in testing one’s own inherent resilience and mental 
robustness, when shortcomings are laid bare in front of 
superiors, peers and subordinates alike, should not be 
underestimated, regardless of the outcome of the mission. 
Finally, we should match our focus and expectation of 
collective training to our own and our enemies’ future 
capabilities. With an increasing focus on STRIKE and 
its need to operate in small teams at reach, being able to 
self-reflect, identify our own mistakes and learn to adapt - 
quickly and quite possibly in the face of the enemy - will 
be of paramount importance. Therefore we must greet
mistakes made in training with optimism, embrace them
3 British Army Review No 170, Autumn/Winter 2017, p7
and reward persistence if we’re to meet subsequent success 
on the battlefield over extended lines of communication. 
Accepting and learning from mission failure in training 
will go some way to fill a vacuum of current enemy 
capabilities which we are not able to train against, 
as outlined by Commander Field Army in BAR 170.3 
Against the backdrop of the true threats we will face on 
today’s battlefield such as massed commercially-available 
drones, a credible and nuisance EW threat, rudimentary 
but credible CBRN threats, massed fires and GPS denial, 
the need to push our training threshold beyond mission 
failure is undeniable.
SUMMARY
There’s no doubt we are improving our collective training, 
but there is still more to do. We should re-calibrate what 
our expectations from collective training are - a learning 
rather than a pass/fail culture; one where we strive for 
excellence whilst not letting this cloud our judgment and 
treatment of poor battlefield discipline, poor leadership, 
sub-standard drills and a feedback-resistant culture. 
It’s a matter of perceptions and leadership - train hard, 
fail harder, learn more and succeed.

EDUCATION
M
ore soldiers1 than ever before are gaining degrees 
in the Army; so why did they fail to achieve their 
potential at school?2 To better understand this apparent 
paradox, I spent a year talking to enlisted men and 
women to try and make some sense of it.
I failed my GCSEs when I was fifteen, a traumatic event 
which led to me joining the Army. The biggest factor 
affecting this bold decision was the fact that I believed 
that the Army was the only organisation that would allow 
me to feel less ashamed of my GCSE results and status 
of ‘confirmed thicko’ which had been drummed into to 
me throughout eleven years of formal education. Happily 
though, years later I gained a first-class honours degree 
that forced me to ask myself the uncomfortable question; 
what happened at school? By engaging in this research, 
I had hoped to find out about the experiences of other 
enlisted soldiers who go on to achieve academically in 
the Army. I wanted to know, if like me, these people failed 
at school or whether the majority of them succeeded at 
school to begin with; is this why they were able to finally 
realise themselves as scholars? 
What follows is an engaged response as an interested 
participant to the interviews I conducted with my three 
primary research subjects, three serving soldiers who 
have achieved a foundation degree qualification or higher 
who are known as P1, P2 and P3. 
1) How do enlisted soldiers evaluate their experiences 
at school?
I didn’t really have any troubles at school...home life for 
me was pretty hard. I was abused by my step-father and 
that’s when I went to live with my nan and grandad. (P2).
I learned only recently that I went to the joint-worst 
school in London.3 My failure in education was 
compounded by a traumatic home-life. I began my 
questioning in this area because I wanted to understand 
the similarities and differences between mine and

I decided to turn my focus to the value of ‘school’ both in

‘I’m from a working class so my culture where I grew

As working-class children understand and internalise

CONCLUSIONS
a) Context at home and social class
The research confirmed that background plays a pivotal 
role in educational achievement. This factor proved 
instrumental for both those children who experience a 
traumatic home life whilst attending a good school as 
well as those who are happy at home but come from a 
firm working-class background. The case of the latter is 
the more typical story of many young people who enlist 
into the Army but this profile is not exclusive. Regardless 
of the reasons for failing at school, the Army continues to 
offer these people a career where individuals are judged 
not by their exam results but by the effort they put in.
b) Success as a compulsory learner vs 
enlisted volunteer 
The research data confirmed that some enlisted folk 
were only able to succeed academically once they had 
left mainstream compulsory education. In some cases 
it was the experience of failing in school that led to a 
redoubling of efforts in the Army whilst in others, there 
was an expectation that a career in the military was 
inevitable post school meaning that GCSE results were 
of little consequence. On a personal level, the Army felt 
like a fresh chance or rather, a last chance, since I had 
failed for so long at school. Moving from a compulsory 
existence to being a volunteer was a powerful shift for 
many young people and this, coupled with the ‘robust’ 
encouragement the Army offered unlocked the potential 
in a way that state schooling couldn’t.
c) Does Army training yield better results 
Regardless of antecedent causes, all participants reported 
that they found it easier to succeed in the Army compared 
to school. In some cases this was attributed to schools 
failing to cater for preferred learning styles but more 
commonly, this phenomena was connected to a collective 
experience of motivated peers. Despite training being 
described as being ‘brutal’, each of the participants believe 
that this was appropriate, ‘it had to be that way’. 
The element of competition encouraged these enlisted 
men to strive to be the best they could be, motivated by

LAST THOUGHTS
The Army has a mechanism whereby soldiers leaving the 
Army are given training to become teachers when they 
become civilians.8 It is apparent that schools value those 
skills and qualities that soldiers possess in abundance; 
team work, determination and powers of discipline. It is 
also worthy of note that the precursor to state education 
belonged to the Army, as soldiers’ children were educated 
in schools that were funded by the Commanding Officer 
of their regiments. Indeed, the Army was investing in 
education as early as 16449, long before the government 
eventually followed suit in 1833 by allocating funding 
for schools. Based on this information, and the fact 
that learners are far more likely to thrive in a military 
environment, surely it would make sense for the Army 
to reinstate the position of Sergeant Schoolmasters into 
the floundering schools of today as part of a new defence 
engagement initiative?

The Dieppe Raid: Part 2: 
The German Response
In Part Two of the story about the German Perspective of the Dieppe 
Raid, Graham Thomas provides a brief narrative of the Allied actions 
and illustrates the German response to those actions. 
Light naval craft covering the landing during the Combined Operations daylight raid on Dieppe. MGB 321 is nearest the camera (partly obscured 
by some sailors in the foreground) whilst submarine chaser Q 014 can be seen in the middle distance. This is photograph A 11234 from the 
collections of the Imperial War Museums. Public domain, Wikimedia

 BAR HISTORY | 101
HISTORY
A
s with Part 1 of this three part series, much of the 
information comes from the German perspective 
of the Allied attack at Dieppe that took place on 19th 
August 1942. In this part, we look at the German 
responses to the Allied landings at Dieppe and how 
they organised their defences. To put this into context 
it is necessary first of all to provide a brief narrative of 
the action. The landings at Dieppe were made up of a 
large contingent of Canadians with British and other 
Commonwealth nationalities involved. The Germans 
refer to this allied force as simply British forces. 
Here they will be referred to as Allies. 
Just prior to the landings at Dieppe, at 0500hrs the Allied 
force engaged a German convoy that alerted the German 
coastal defence system. While the German defenders were 
still unsure as to the whether the ships in front of Dieppe 
were friendly or enemy the answer came with a series 
of air attacks that began at dawn. These attacks were 
directed at defensive positions on both sides of Dieppe. 
These bombing and strafing attacks were meant to pin 
down the enemy defences and while that was taking place 
swarms of landing craft in waves of 40 to 50 headed for 
the shore, coming out of the protection of the morning fog 
and smoke screens laid down by the attacking aircraft and 
naval fire from the destroyers offshore. German artillery 
fire was unable to destroy the Allied landing craft due to 
the smoke screens. The only time that artillery and heavy 
weapons hits were registered on the landing craft was 
as they touched down on the beach. Yet, fog and smoke 
made visibility on the beaches difficult as well. 
At Berneval, east of Dieppe, the British landed a 
Commando force numbering 250 men who took up 
positions in a defile. Their task was to seize and destroy 
the 2nd Battery of the 770th Army Coast Artillery 
Battalion. Using rope ladders and guylines the British 
commandos climbed up the ravine to the top of the 
cliffs, avoiding the minefields that had been placed in 
the ravine. They managed to attack the battery located 
in a fortified strongpoint. One German machine gun 
patrol was dispatched from the battery and moved 
to the ravine where they were able to take part in the 
local defence. The Battery managed to ward off a 
series of uncoordinated British attacks helped by their 
attached army anti-aircraft gun platoon. The ability of

Major Von Blucher, commander of the German 302nd 
Anti-Tank Battalion, was ordered to launch an attack on 
Berneval by HQ 302nd Infantry Division. In addition to 
his existing command he was also given command of the 
Bicycle Squadron from St Nicholas and the attached 3rd 
Pioneer Company, both of which were later reinforced by 
the 3rd Company of the 572nd Infantry Regiment. The 
battery at Berneval had managed to send messages via 
wireless regarding the disposition of the British close 
attacks enabling von Blucher to launch a successful 
1 Report No 116, Operation Jubillee, The Raid on Dieppe, 19 August 1942, Additional Information from German Sources, Directorate of History, 
 
National Defence Headquarters, Ottawa, Canada
counter-attack against the British commandos that 
resulted in 2 officers and 80 men being taken prisoner. 
West of Dieppe, the German 813th Army Coastal Battery 
was situated at Varengeville. Against this target the 
British launched an attack with 300 Commandos. 
They landed on both sides of Varengeville at the base of 
the cliffs under the cover of a smoke screen. Elsewhere, 
another company of commandos landed near the fortified 
strongpoints at Quiberville, against a platoon from 
the 3rd Company 571st Infantry Regiment. However, 
the Germans frustrated this attack with concentrated 
machine gun and rifle fire. While these forces were 
pinned down the attack at Varengeville was going well 
and turned out to be a success for the British. Here the 
commandos climbed the cliffs aided by small, wooded, 
rugged ravines stretching down to the sea.1 
Two of the landing craft, one containing a Bren-carrier, alongside a destroyer after returning from the beaches during the Combined Operations 
daylight raid on Dieppe. The landing craft mechanised are (left to right) LCM (1) 169 and LCM (1) 2 © IWM (A 11228)

 BAR HISTORY | 103
Once they’d reached the top of the cliffs the British 
commandos attacked the German battery from all sides 
using machine guns, sub-machine guns, rifles, mortars 
and grenades. At the same time, RAF fighters and fighter 
bombers pounded the battery with bombs and cannon fire 
stopping the defenders from mounting any real defence 
against the commandos. The German losses amounted to 
28 dead and 29 wounded (according to this report).2 The 
German battery commander who was directing fire from 
the observation post was one of those wounded during this 
action. ‘Later, accompanied by the observation section, he 
fought his way towards the fighting Battery.’3 Shells stored 
in the ammunition pits, the battery emplacement and in 
the guns themselves ignited from the aerial bombing and 
mortar fire causing several explosions and setting the guns 
on fire, making them unusable. The British re-embarked 
at approximately 0900 hours taking their wounded and 
dead with them, including some German prisoners. 
Both operations, at Berneval and at Varengeville, 
obviously had as their mission the destruction of the 
two heavy coastal batteries. This would have facilitated 
further debarkations and embarkations at Dieppe.4 
The Germans knew that both coastal batteries were 
vulnerable but the lack of available troops meant that 
both batteries could not be given special protection by 
the infantry. In addition, the Germans realised that the 
main Allied attack on Dieppe was developing on a broad 
front with three main thrusts at the village of Puys, at 
Dieppe itself and at Pourville. 
At Puys the Allied landings collapsed under heavy 
concentrated fire from the German defences, with 
heavy losses. Indeed, not one Allied soldier managed 
to penetrate these defences and move forwards. 
‘The flanking fire in front of the obstacles, on the high 
sea wall, and on the beach itself decimated his attacking 
lines. Aside from the numerous prisoners, over 150 dead 
were counted at this point.’5

Locust moved into the harbour approaches at 0700hrs

Two Allied battalions landed on the beach at Dieppe 
itself, reinforced by tanks, and tried to make their way off 
the beach up to the promenade.7 The tanks were either 
destroyed as they landed or, as a few of them managed to 
get to the beach promenade, they were then hit by heavy 
artillery fire. Only a few patrols managed to penetrate into 
the town. 
The sixth Battalion8 that landed had greater success in 
its landings and were, under the cover of darkness and 
fog able to penetrate into Pourville in the west, where 
they attacked and overpowered the garrison stationed 
there. The Allies then tried to move forwards and reach 
its objectives with two companies moving west out 
of Pourville along the coastal road towards the Scie 
Valley where they successfully attacked several German 
positions. ‘They succeeded in getting as far as the anti-
tank position which they disabled temporarily by direct 
hits, and possibly by hand grenades.’9 Some Allied patrols 
managed to get as far as the Scie Dam10 but when they 
attempted to advance towards the northern part of 4 
Ventes Farm11, a heavily defended German strongpoint, 
they were wiped out. As such both companies, while 
having advanced the furthest were unable to penetrate 
the main line of German resistance. ‘The main Dieppe 
defences really began at this anti-tank position. Pourville 
was only a lightly held advanced outpost.’12

The two other companies of the sixth Battalion13 operated 
west of the Scie River where they managed to attain their 
first objectives. They seized the southern edge of Pourville 
and the machine gun position on the hill west of Pourville, 
where they established a bridgehead. 
The seventh Allied Battalion14 was to follow in the sixth 
Battalion’s wake and push forward towards the west bank 
of the Scie and capture its main objective, the airfield 
at St Aubin. This battalion also reached Pourville and 
managed to advance in close wooded country on the hills 
west of the Scie as far as Hautot where it was caught in 
the flanking fire from 4 Ventes Farm. ‘It then encountered 
the forward Bicycle Platoon of the Regimental 
Headquarters of the 571st Infantry Regiment and some 
patrols from the 1st Battalion of the same Regiment.’15 
Up to that point the seventh Allied battalion had not 
encountered real German opposition as there were very 
little defences set up in the area. However, it wasn’t

GERMAN DEFENSIVE ACTION
The Germans soon became aware of the full scope of 
the attack a little after 0600hrs when it became apparent 
that no attacks were taking place at the mouth of the 
Somme in Le Treport or in the area under control of 532nd 
Infantry Division. As a result the Division dispatched the 
Bicycle Troop and the reinforced 3rd Pioneer Company to 
Berneval from Marques-La-Bataille. As we have seen these 
forces were commanded by Major Von Blucher and were 
ordered to relieve the Berneval battery then under attack. 
The First Battalion of the 571st Infantry Regiment, then 
in Dieppe, was ordered to leave Quiberville around 
0710hrs and move to Hutot in order to counter the Allied 
attack in the direction of Pourville. 
At 0730hrs the 3rd Battalion of 570th Infantry Regiment 
came under command of 302nd Infantry Division and 
was ordered to Offrenville while the remainder, 676th 
Infantry Regiment HQ, its 1st and 3rd Battalions, 1st 
Battalion of the 332nd Artillery Regiment, and the 81st 
Tank Company were ordered to move to Bacqueville, 
14 kilometres southeast of Dieppe. 
In the Hutot area, around 1000hrs, the 1st Battalion of 
the 571st Infantry began preparing for a counter attack 
on British positions in Pourville. However, because of the 
close country, fighting would be difficult and unfamiliar. 
To remedy this, the battalion mounted a reconnaissance 
in the direction of Pourville and Varengeville opening its 
attack on Pourville around 1130hrs. The result of this 
attack enabled it to clear the hill west of Pourville of Allied 
soldiers where 200 prisoners were taken.
In the meantime, all the Corps reserves were now under 
command of 302nd Infantry Division in order to mount an 
attack out of Offrenville towards Pourville supported by 
tanks from the 81st Tank Company. However, this attack 
never took place because the 1st Battalion of the 571st 
Infantry Regiment had already cleared the British and 
Commonwealth troops out of the area west of Pourville.

In the afternoon, the 676th Infantry Regiment was 
deployed to the Pourville - St Aubin sector where it 
committed two battalions and held one in reserve. 
At this time there were several messages reporting 
large formations of ships arriving from England and the 
Germans believed there was a possibility that the Allied 
attack would be renewed.
The 10th Armoured Division, now nominally under 
the command of LXXXI Corps was ordered to move 
its advanced units as quickly as possible up to an area 
14 kilometres south of Dieppe. The rest of the division 
was then ordered into the Neufchatel - Londinieres 
area. According to the German sources, the intention 
of the German commanders was to position the 10th 
Armoured Division west of the Argues River to attack the 
British and Canadian units that had landed at Pourville. 
However, the decision to commit the 10th Armoured into 
this area depended on whether other German forces had 
been successful in pushing the enemy at Pourville back 
into the sea. If that was the case, the 10th Armoured 
were to be deployed to the East.
 
The following orders were issued to the 10th Armoured 
Division and the 302nd Infantry Division at 1200 hrs:
• The 10th Armoured Division with its advanced elements 
and those units already committed from the 302nd 
Infantry Division and Corps Reserves, first attack the 
heights west of Pourville. It is to destroy the enemy, and 
then join in the attack from the West of, and in, Dieppe, 
if this is necessary. 
• Boundary between the 302nd and the 10th Divisions: 
from the Western edge of Pourville to Janvall to the 
SCIE Valley. 
• Those parts of the 302nd Infantry Division and Corps 
Reserve that have already advanced to the West of this 
line will be attached to the 10th Armoured Division.

Who Were The Chindits?
Captain Dominic Selwood, 77X, provides a brief history of Orde 
Wingate and the Chindits and outlines their contribution to the British 
victory over the Japanese in Burma during the Second World War. 
Chindits places explosive charges on a railway bridge behind Japanese lines in Burma, 1944 © IWM (SE 7921)
A far from prepossessing lot we were. No badges of rank were worn - nor were any pay books or identity 
cards carried - and officers and men had the same cut-throat appearance. Beards of all colours and lengths 
were on display. Our dress was uniform in only one respect - its dark green colour. Some there were whose 
trousers were raggedly cut down to shorts - a practice not much in favour because of the thorny undergrowth; 
some dispensed with shirts altogether and wore only cotton vests so much easier to dry than a shirt after a 
day's march in pouring rain; bush hats of all shapes were worn at all angles, all much battered after being 
used as pillows and ‘fire-blowers’. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Chindit Cipher Corporal, Operation THURSDAY (1944)

 BAR HISTORY | 109
T
he ‘Chindits’ were a British Indian Army special 
forces unit that operated in World War Two. While 
David Stirling and his fledgling SAS were pioneering 
long-range penetration behind enemy lines in the deserts 
of North Africa, the Chindits were doing the same in the 
treacherous jungles of Burma (Myanmar). 
The brain behind the Chindits was the British Artillery 
officer Orde Wingate - one of the most unlikely and 
maverick commanders of the war. As well as coming up 
with the idea of long-range penetration behind Japanese 
lines, he stamped the Chindits with his energy, grit, and 
determination to push troops to the limits of endurance.
ORDE WINGATE
Orde Wingate was born in Nainital, British India, in 
the foothills of the Himalayas. His father’s and mother’s 
families were both military, and strongly Christian. 
Wingate was raised as a member of the Plymouth 
Brethren, which gave him a strong belief in the literal 
truth of the Bible, and a durable sense of not conforming 
with the views of mainstream society. He was home-
schooled, then sent to Charterhouse, before attending 
the Royal Military Academy Woolwich, where he was not 
successful, and did not fit in. 
Wingate was commissioned into the Royal Artillery in 
1923. Five years later he transferred to the Sudan Defence 
Force, where he spent another five years, before moving 
to an intelligence role in Palestine. 
In the Near East, facing the Arab Revolt (1936-9), he 
tried his hand at irregular warfare, experimenting with 
organizing mixed British-Jewish groups into highly 
flexible and mobile light units he called Special Night 
Squads. The tactic turned out to be effective, in much 
the same way as the guerrilla strategies of T E Lawrence 
had been in the Arabian desert two decades earlier. 
(Wingate and Lawrence were, in fact, distant relatives.)
The success of these Special Night Squads was a 
turning point for Wingate, who discovered that he thrived 
on planning and executing special operations.

(Wingate and Lawrence were, in fact, distant relatives.)
The success of these Special Night Squads was a 
turning point for Wingate, who discovered that he thrived 
on planning and executing special operations. He was, 
however, a complex character, and while in Palestine 
developed an intense fervour for Zionism. His lifelong 
attachment to the Old Testament had convinced him he 
was a man of religious destiny. As a child he fantasized 
he was Oliver Cromwell, with a sword in one hand and a 
Bible in the other.
Once in Palestine, Wingate came to believe that it was 
his fate to train and lead a Jewish Army into battle. 
This dream and overt involvement in Palestinian 
politics caused him increasing problems with the 
establishment, as did his slovenly dress, disrespect 
for authority, unshakeable self-belief, and fondness for 
reading Old Testament Scripture to his troops. 
Wingate was, however, fortunate to have the support 
and protection of Archibald Wavell, General Officer 
Commanding Palestine and Transjordan. When Wavell 
moved from Palestine to become Commander-in-Chief 
Middle East, he deployed Wingate to Abyssinia (Ethiopia) 
to support an insurgency against the occupying Italian 
forces. In this role, Wingate drew on his experiences with 
the Special Night Squads, and organized his Sudanese 
regulars and Abyssinian levies into an irregular army. 
His biblical hero was Gideon, who won a decisive victory 
while heavily outnumbered, and Wingate named his 
1,700 troops ‘Gideon Force’. 
Brigadier Orde Wingate in India after returning from operations in 
Japanese-occupied Burma with his Chindits unit in 1943 
© IWM (IND 2237)

110 | The British Army Review 174: Winter 2019
The group nominally came under the command of 
the Special Operations Executive (SOE), and among 
its notable member was Wilfred Thesiger, who had 
commissioned as a Bimbashi in the Sudan Defence Force 
in order to help rid his birthplace of the Italians. 
Wingate instructed Gideon Force in irregular tactics, and 
it proved highly successful, outsmarting and defeating 
far larger Italian forces. His moment of glory came when 
Gideon Force escorted Emperor Haile Selassie into Addis 
Ababa and placed him back on his throne. 
During this period Wingate became an ardent supporter 
of the cult of Selassie (Rastafarianism), whose members 
believed Selassie was a living god and the second 
coming of Christ. As with his Zionism, Wingate’s 
religious zeal in this earned him the animosity of his 
colleagues and superiors, who questioned his judgement 
and motivation.
Bad luck and a lack of manpower dogged Wavell 
throughout the war, and Churchill was not a fan of his, 
although others were. Rommel treasured his copy of 
Wavell’s General and Generalship, and carried it with him 
throughout the North Africa campaign. 
Unhappy with progress, Churchill relieved Wavell 
of his Middle East command, and sent him to India. 
With his protector gone, Wingate was ordered to Cairo, 
where he fell into a profound depression at losing his 
command, and at his superiors’ refusal to accept his 
recommendations for Abyssinia, or his requests for 
Haile Selassie, Emperor of Abyssinia, with Brigadier Daniel Arthur Sandford (left) and Colonel Wingate (right) in Dambacha Fort, 
after it had been captured, 15 April 1941

decorations to be awarded to the men of Gideon Force. 
While laid up in the Continental Hotel suffering from a 
high malarial fever, he attempted suicide by stabbing 
himself twice in the neck with a Bowie knife. 
Lieutenant Colonel Cudbert Thornhill of MI6/SOE was 
in the next room. He recalled that he was usually relaxed 
if he heard someone lock a door. He was also relaxed 
if he heard someone fall over. But if he heard both then 
‘something had to be done’. He broke down Wingate’s 
door, and managed to get medical assistance in time to 
save Wingate’s life.
THE CHINDITS
In India. Wavell found himself facing a confident Japan 
to the east, emboldened by the British collapse in Malaya 
(Malaysia) and Burma. Remembering the Special Night 
Squads and Gideon Force, he sent for Wingate. 
On arrival in India, Wingate teamed up with Major 
Michael Calvert, a British officer who had also been born 
in India. The two saw eye-to-eye on questions of strategy, 
and conducted a reconnaissance of Burma, after which 
Wingate settled on the idea of a long-range penetration 
force. He envisaged creating mobile light infantry units, 
connected by sophisticated wireless communications, 
and resupplied by airdrops. He believed that such groups 
would be able to penetrate deep into the Burmese jungle, 
slip through the Japanese defences, and disrupt their 
communication and supply lines.

Wavell liked the idea, and allocated a British battalion 
and a Gurkha battalion to the project. Wingate broke up 
the men’s traditional regimental framework and instead 
organized the force into columns - each effectively an 
infantry company of around 400 men, complete with 
signallers, other specialists, and mules. The force was 
officially named the 77th Indian Infantry Brigade, but 
Wingate nicknamed them the ‘Chindits’, which was a 
mispronunciation of Chinthe - the Burmese mythical lion-
griffin that stood guard outside many of the country’s 
pagodas. This creature, standing by a miniature pagoda, 
became their badge.
OPERATION LONGCLOTH
The Chindits trained intensively until, by early February 
1943, they were ready to deploy on their first mission 
into Burma. The regular troops who were supposed to 
follow behind them pulled out, but Wingate convinced 
Wavell to allow the Chindits to go in order to prove the 
concept of long-range penetration. Wavell consented. 
And so, on 8 February, 3,000 Chindits divided into seven 
columns headed out from their forward operating base 
at Imphal in Manipur, 40 miles west of the Burmese 
border. Northern Group - the main Chindit force - 
marched northeast into Burma. The smaller Southern 
Group - acting as a decoy, receiving its airdrops in broad 
daylight - headed southeast, with plans for both groups 
to converge deep inside the jungle.

The men had to cope not only with the jungle conditions 
and the presence of the enemy, but around 100 lbs of kit 
each, including 1937 pattern webbing, Everest back pack, 
compass, maps, water bottle, canvas water container, five 
days’ rations, mess tins and utensils, clothing, bedding, 
towel, sewing and shaving kits, first aid pack, silver 
rupees, Lee Enfield rifle with 50 rounds, Bren gun, five 
Bren magazines, grenades, bayonet, and dah machete. 
Some platoons also had Vickers machine guns, anti-tank 
weapons and flamethrowers. Officers additionally carried 
sidearms, flare pistols, and torches. 
Both groups successfully crossed the Chindwin River, 
sneaked through the Japanese lines, and began their pre-
planned acts of sabotage and disruption. A particularly 
important and strategic target was the main north-
south Myitkyina–Mandalay railway. It was crucial to the 
Japanese supply operation, and the Chindits successfully 
located it and destroyed it at multiple points. 
The battle is not always to the strong nor the race to 
the swift.1 
Wingate then amended the operation, and ordered the 
Chindits over the Irrawaddy River and deeper into Burma. 
1 Orde Wingate Order of the Day 13 February 1943
However, the terrain proved highly challenging, there were 
few water supplies, and they were at the extreme limit of 
air resupply. With the Japanese closing in, Wingate broke 
the columns up into smaller dispersal units, and ordered 
them to make their way separately back to India. 
The return journey was gruelling. The Japanese were 
everywhere, and the two river crossings left the Chindits 
highly vulnerable to attack or capture. To compound 
the difficulties, many were suffering from exhaustion, 
dysentery, and tropical diseases. What was left of the 
groups eventually trickled back into India. Of the 3,000 
men who had set out, only 2,000 returned, of whom only 
600 were declared fit to continue military service.
HEROES
There was not much good news coming from Wavell’s 
Indian HQ at the time, but Churchill quickly latched 
onto Operation LONGCLOTH, publicizing it widely 
as a triumph. The newspapers seized on the story, 
describing excitedly how a small force of Chindits had 
outmanoeuvred the Imperial Japanese Army, causing 
it to waste time and valuable resources hunting them 
down, distracting it from its military priorities, and 
inflicting damage on its infrastructure. 
Chindits prepare a road block to protect their bivouac against Japanese attack. © IWM (IND 2078)

Although the sabotaged railway and communications 
were repaired before long, the Chindits had turned the 
tables, and seized the military initiative. They shattered 
the myth that the Japanese were invincible in the jungle, 
and proved that a band of British and Commonwealth 
troops was more than capable of beating the Japanese. 
The Chindits were the heroes of the moment, and the 
morale of British troops in India soared.

into the hot seat. He expanded the Chindits to a corps-
sized force, gave Wingate a hotline to Downing Street, 
and a supportive Supreme Commander South East Asia

was also put under Wingate’s command, along with a full 
U.S. air task force of fighters, bombers, and transports.
As Wingate set about training up his enlarged Chindit 
force - now the 3rd Indian Infantry Division - he did not 
always win friends and allies among his colleagues and 
men. Despite his ample courage, energy, and vision, 
he was also capable of being imperious, ruthless, 
insubordinate, and pig-headed: traits which earned him 
admiration and animosity in equal measures. He was

The new plan was for the Chindits to lead the way into 
Burma, followed by General Slim’s 14th Army, which 
would be able to deploy heavy firepower to hold captured 
ground. However, on catching wind of the planned 
Japanese attack on India, Slim pulled his troops out of 
the project and instead deployed them in defensive roles. 
Wingate decided to press ahead anyway and go it alone 
with the Chindits. 
OPERATION THURSDAY
The Chindits headed back into Burma on 5 March 1944 
(three months and one day before D-Day). The original 
77th Brigade was now commanded by Wingate’s 
number two, Lieutenant Colonel Michael Calvert, and 
was accompanied by five other brigades. All together, 
they were known as Special Force. 
The Chindits were again divided into columns, each 
numbering around 400 men and made up of four infantry 
platoons, a heavy weapons platoon with Vickers machine 
guns, mortars, and anti-tank weapons, a commando 
platoon, a reconnaissance platoon, sappers, signallers, 
medics, and mules.

The plan required 83 Dakotas to tow multiple gliders to 
three pre-selected landing sites - Broadway, Chowringhee, 
and Piccadilly - which would then be prepared for the 
arrival of transport planes. Despite initial confusion 
and setbacks, the insertion was largely successful, and 
Churchill sent a congratulatory telegram for what had been 
the largest airborne operation in British military history. 
The Chindits moved off into the jungle to establish fortified 
bases codenamed Aberdeen, Blackpool, Broadway, and 
White City. The Japanese attacked in force, and there was 
intense fighting around the strongholds, often hand-to-
hand with bayonets and khukuris against katanas. Where 
possible, the Chindits broke out from their strongholds to 
conduct sabotage against the Japanese infrastructure.
 
However, three weeks into the operation, a U.S. B-25 
bomber Wingate was travelling in near Imphal crashed, 
killing all passengers. 
The Allies have lost one of the most forceful and 
dynamic personalities that this war has produced. 
You have lost the finest and most inspiring leader 
a force could have wished for. He has lit the torch. 
Together we must grasp it and carry it forward.2

operation was highly personal, and brigade commanders 
were left to second guess what Wingate would have 
done. Meanwhile, Stilwell had not fully appreciated 
that the Chindits were trained and organized for light 
irregular warfare. Instead, he deployed them in regular 
engagements for which they were unsuited and ill-

sustained during this period under Stilwell’s command. 
The 2,000 remaining men of 77th Brigade were ordered 
to attack the 4,000-strong Japanese base at Mogaung. 
The Brigade succeeded, won two VCs, but was left with 
only 300 fit men standing - one of whom was Major 
James Lumley, officer in the 6th Gurkha Rifles, and father 
of actress Joanna Lumley. Other Chindit brigades faced 
similar fates.
Alarmed, Mountbatten intervened, and ordered the 
Chindits back to India. The last one left Burma on 27 
August 1944. They had been in the jungle for 175 days, 
although Wingate had always stipulated an outside limit 
of 90 days for any operation.
Exhausted, malnourished, and riddled with diseases, the 
columns fought their way west to the Indian border. Many 
died on the journey. Those too unwell to move were left 
with Burmese villagers. Of those who came out of the 
jungle alive, half required immediate hospitalisation. 
The death toll was high, although not on the relative level 
of Operation LONGCLOTH the previous year.3 
BACK IN INDIA
When recovered, those Chindits fit enough began 
training again. But when Calvert was flown back to 
England in March 1945 with a damaged Achilles tendon, 
the Chindits were unexpectedly disbanded. On release 
from hospital, Calvert was instead given command of 
the SAS (David Stirling was a prisoner of war in Colditz 
Castle) until it was disbanded in October 1945. When 
it was reformed in 1950 as the Malayan Scouts (SAS), 
Calvert was again given command.

ASSESSMENT
The Chindits were founded in 1942 and broken up in 1945. 
They were operationally active from 1943–4, undertaking 
two missions. They pushed the limits of long-range 
penetration further than ever before, and established that 
irregular light troops could operate effectively in the jungle 
behind enemy lines with supplies delivered by air. In this, 
they and Wingate join the likes of Gordon of Khartoum, 
Lawrence of Arabia, and Colin Gubbins of the SOE as 
pioneers in British irregular warfare.
Their memory lives on in many ways, including in the 
Chindit Society, the Burma Star Association, and the 
memorial on Victoria Embankment outside the Ministry 
of Defence in London, which celebrates the international 
nature of the Chindits, noting they came from the United 
Kingdom, Burma, Hong Kong, India, Nepal, West Africa, 
and the United States of America. 
 
Churchill’s epitaph to Wingate is also carved into the 
stone: ‘A man of genius who might well have become a 
man of destiny’. 
Commentators continue to debate the pros and cons of 
special forces - whether they deliver necessary skills to

selected individuals. Whatever the historical ebb and flow 
of the special forces debate, the Chindits earned their place 
in the history of special operations with some of the most 
daring and arduous exploits of any modern fighting force.
 
77th BRIGADE
The Chindits are also honoured in the modern British 
Army’s 77th Brigade, which was raised in January 2015 to 
challenge the difficulties of modern warfare using non-
lethal engagement to adapt the behaviour of adversaries.

77th BRIGADE
The Chindits are also honoured in the modern British 
Army’s 77th Brigade, which was raised in January 2015 to 
challenge the difficulties of modern warfare using non-
lethal engagement to adapt the behaviour of adversaries. 
It is not an infantry brigade, but is built on notable elements 
of the Chindits’ spirit, including operating behind enemy 
lines in the Information Activity and Outreach spaces, 
and in deploying strategies that seek to use specialist 
skills to achieve disproportionately large effects. 
To honour the heritage of the original Chindits, it has 
taken the number 77, and its members wear an updated 
version of the Chinthe lion-griffin badge. Although the 
77th Brigade does not claim - or aspire - to be a recreation 
of Wingate’s Chindits, it is proud to keep alive the memory 
of that extraordinarily unconventional, courageous, and 
pioneering force.
